AI can act exactly like a human, but we still don't think it's conscious

📅 14 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (863 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Even when artificial intelligence behaves exactly like a human, people are reluctant to consider it conscious, according to a new study from Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich (LMU).
  • As artificial intelligence becomes more advanced, reports of AI systems misleading customers, working together, or appearing to pursue independent goals are becoming increasingly common.
  • New research from LMU suggests that people make a clear distinction between displaying intelligent behavior and possessing a conscious mind, even when humans and AI act in precisely the same way.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Even when artificial intelligence behaves exactly like a human, people are reluctant to consider it conscious, according to a new study from Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich (LMU).

As artificial intelligence becomes more advanced, reports of AI systems misleading customers, working together, or appearing to pursue independent goals are becoming increasingly common. These behaviors often lead people to describe AI as though it can think, feel, or make decisions for itself. But does behaving like a human actually convince people that a machine has consciousness?

New research from LMU suggests that people make a clear distinction between displaying intelligent behavior and possessing a conscious mind, even when humans and AI act in precisely the same way.

How Scientists Tested Perceptions of AI Consciousness.

Published in the journal Cognition, the study was led by Dr. Louis Longin of LMU's Chair of Philosophy of Mind, working alongside Dr. Bahador Bahrami, Professor Ophelia Deroy, and other researchers.

"Whereas previous studies have typically asked general questions about whether AI actually has mental states, our study is the first to directly compare how people attribute the same mental states to AI and humans behaving in exactly the same way, under identical circumstances," states Longin.

Industry observers note that "We may be using mental terms to refer to AI, but this may only be because we lack better words," says Ophelia Deroy, philosopher and a senior author of the study. "After all, AI is trained to act and speak like a human, so these descriptions seem natural.".

To investigate how people judge consciousness, the researchers conducted experiments involving nearly 1,100 participants. One group read brief descriptions of artificial agents that showed different levels of responsiveness to their environments. For example, some agents reacted to sounds or recognized the emotional states of others.

Another group encountered the same situations, except the characters were described as humans rather than AI systems. Participants then evaluated how conscious or aware each character seemed to be of its surroundings.

A Surprising Gap Between Human and AI Consciousness.

The experiments revealed that responsiveness influenced how participants judged both humans and artificial intelligence. Characters that reacted more actively to their surroundings were generally considered more conscious and more aware.

It has been revealed that however, a striking difference emerged when participants evaluated consciousness specifically. Even the most responsive AI was rated as less conscious than the least responsive human. In other words, identical behavior did not lead people to assign the same level of consciousness to humans and machines.

The results changed considerably when participants were asked about awareness instead. For this characteristic, judgments of humans and AI followed largely similar patterns, suggesting that people interpret awareness and consciousness in fundamentally different ways.

"There is a growing worry in public discussion that people will see AI behaving in a human-like way and start treating these systems as if they had human-like mental states," claims Longin, lead author of the study. "We found something much more nuanced: People are quite willing to say that an AI notices things and is aware of its surroundings. But they clearly draw a line when it comes to the term 'consciousness'. People consistently attribute less consciousness to AI than humans -- even when their behavior is identical.".

Although people sometimes describe AI as conscious when discussing its actions, the findings indicate that they still distinguish between artificial systems and human minds.

Why One Word Changes How We Perceive AI.

The researchers believe the difference between consciousness and awareness offers an notable insight into how people understand artificial intelligence.

Awareness is a relatively neutral term that can describe an agent's ability to detect and respond to information in its environment. Consciousness, however, carries deeper implications about subjective experience and what it means to have an inner mental life.

Because awareness focuses more directly on observable behavior, people appear comfortable applying it to both humans and AI. Consciousness carries a different meaning, leading people to judge the two much less similarly.

The findings also highlight why the language used to discuss artificial intelligence matters, particularly as AI systems become increasingly capable of producing convincing human behavior.

Sources indicate that "Our study teaches us lessons for how we communicate about AI," says Bahador Bahrami, who is also a senior author of the study and an expert in social neuroscience. "Companies and journalists often reach for hyped descriptions of AI models, and credit them with intentions, plans, or even moral conscience and hesitation. What our study indicates is that everyday judgments are much more discriminating: People do not simply put AI and humans on the same mental scale. But the boundary also depends on which terms we use. For more neutral descriptors such as 'awareness', the distinction can largely disappear. That makes our choice of language important.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that gradio is an open-source Python package for creating AI-powered web applications. Gradio is compliant with the MCP server protocol and powers thousands of MCP servers hosted on Hugging Face Spaces. The Gradio team is betting significant on Gradio and Spaces being the best way to build and host AI-powered MCP servers.

To that end, here are some of the substantial improvements we've added to Gradio MCP servers as of version 5.38.0.

If you've tried to use a remote Gradio MCP server that takes a file as input (image, video, audio), you've probably encountered this error:.

This happens because the Gradio server is hosted on a different machine, meaning any input files must be accessible via a public URL so they can be downloaded remotely.

Recent findings suggest that while many ways exist to host files online, they all add a manual step to your workflow. In the age of LLM agents, shouldn't we expect them to handle this for you?

Gradio now includes a "File Upload" MCP server that agents can use to upload files directly to your Gradio application. If any tools in your Gradio MCP server require file inputs, the connection documentation will now show you how to start the "File Upload" MCP server:.

Learn more about using this server (and important security considerations) in the Gradio Guides.

Depending on the AI task, getting results can take some time. Now, Gradio streams progress notifications to your MCP client, allowing you to monitor the status in real-time!

As an MCP developer, it's highly recommended to implement your MCP tools to emit these progress statuses. Our guide demonstrates you how.

In a recent development, if you want to integrate an existing backend API into an LLM, you have to manually map API endpoints to MCP tools. This can be a time-consuming and error prone chore. With this release, Gradio can automate the entire process for you! With a single line of code, you can integrate your business backend into any MCP-compatible LLM.

OpenAPI is a widely adopted standard for describing RESTful APIs in a machine-readable format, typically as a JSON file. Gradio now features the gr.load_openapi function, which creates a Gradio application directly from an OpenAPI schema. You can then launch the app with mcp_server=True to automatically create an MCP server for your API!

Find more details in the Gradio Guides.

A common pattern in MCP server development is to use authentication headers to call services on behalf of your consumers. As an MCP server developer, you want to clearly communicate to your users which credentials they need to provide for proper server usage.

To make this possible, you can now type your MCP server arguments as gr.Header. Gradio will automatically extract that header from the incoming request (if it exists) and pass it to your function. The benefit of using gr.Header is that the MCP connection docs will automatically display the headers you need to supply when connecting to the server!

In the example below, the X-API-Token header is extracted from the incoming request and passed in as the x_api_token argument to make_api_request_on_behalf_of_user.

You can read more about this in the Gradio Guides.

It has been revealed that gradio automatically generates tool descriptions from your function names and docstrings. Now you can customize the tool description even further with the api_description parameter. In this example, the tool description will read "Apply a sepia filter to any image.".

According to recent reports, want us to add a new MCP-related feature to Gradio? Let us know in the comments of the blog or on GitHub. Also if you've built a cool MCP server or Gradio app let us know in the comments and we'll amplify it!

#149500. People are taking an unapproved weight-loss drug. AI found something surprising

📅 22 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1443 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

People are taking an unapproved weight-loss drug. AI found something surprising

📅 22 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1443 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • An experimental weight-loss drug that has not yet received regulatory approval is already attracting people willing to obtain unapproved versions online.
  • Sources indicate that the drug, retatrutide, belongs to a new generation of GLP-1 medications designed to help regulate appetite and body weight.
  • Industry observers note that researchers at the University of Pennsylvania analyzed nearly 150,000 Reddit posts and comments from approximately 40,000 consumers to investigate these accounts.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An experimental weight-loss drug that has not yet received regulatory approval is already attracting people willing to obtain unapproved versions online. Now, scientists are using artificial intelligence to investigate their experiences, uncovering unexpected symptom reports that differ from those documented in clinical trials.

Sources indicate that the drug, retatrutide, belongs to a new generation of GLP-1 medications designed to help regulate appetite and body weight. Although it remains under investigation and is not approved for use, people are purchasing unapproved formulations that are not intended for human consumption and discussing their experiences on internet forums.

Industry observers note that researchers at the University of Pennsylvania analyzed nearly 150,000 Reddit posts and comments from approximately 40,000 consumers to investigate these accounts. Their study, published in JAMA Network Open, provides the first systematic examination of potential side effects reported by people claiming to use unapproved retatrutide.

One finding stood out. Among users whose reported symptoms could be classified, increased appetite was the most common complaint. That was particularly unexpected because retatrutide is designed to suppress hunger, and its Phase 2 clinical trials primarily identified digestive problems as the most frequent side effects.

AI Uncovers Unexpected Weight-Loss Drug Reports.

"Our goal is to identify hypotheses in online conversations that we could test. AI helps us find recurring patterns in people's self-reports, including experiences that may be missed by conventional drug-safety monitoring," claims Sharath Chandra Guntuku, Research Associate Professor in Computer and Information Science (CIS), Director of Penn's Computational Social Listening Lab and senior author of the study.

However, the researchers emphasize that the findings should not be interpreted as proof of previously unknown side effects. Reddit users represent a very different population from clinical trial participants, and their accounts cannot establish whether the drug caused the symptoms they described.

According to recent reports, there is also considerable uncertainty about what these individuals are actually taking. Products sold outside regulated medical channels may differ from the genuine experimental medication in their ingredients, purity, and dosage.

"We can't say that retatrutide is causing these symptoms, or even that Reddit users are actually taking genuine retatrutide, since the drug is not legally available, and gray market formulations vary," notes Lyle Ungar, Professor in CIS and a co-author of the study.

Rather than confirming new risks, the research offers scientists an opportunity to identify questions that warrant more rigorous investigation.

"This is the first glimpse into the experiences of a population that is otherwise outside conventional drug safety monitoring because they are taking unapproved versions of a drug that has yet to finish clinical trials," notes Neil Sehgal, the study's first author and a doctoral student in CIS.

How Researchers Analyzed 150,000 Reddit Posts.

The project builds on previous research by the University of Pennsylvania team. In that earlier investigation, scientists used large language models (LLMs), the type of artificial intelligence that powers many modern chatbots, to examine more than 400,000 Reddit posts discussing semaglutide and tirzepatide.

That analysis revealed reports of possible side effects, including menstrual irregularities, that may not have been fully documented in clinical trials or official drug safety records.

"We wanted to apply the same methodology to gray-market retatrutide," notes Sehgal.

Retatrutide is particularly interesting because it works differently from existing GLP-1 medications. Semaglutide acts on one hormone receptor involved in blood sugar control and appetite regulation, while tirzepatide targets two. Retatrutide activates three receptors, potentially producing a different combination of effects throughout the body.

Recent findings suggest that to investigate what people were experiencing, the researchers used AI to examine nearly 150,000 Reddit posts and comments. They identified approximately 14,000 owners who claimed to have personally taken an unapproved version of retatrutide.

The AI systems then extracted descriptions of symptoms that users associated with the medication and translated those descriptions into standardized medical terminology. This allowed researchers to compare reports even when different people used different words to describe similar experiences.

After excluding expected effects such as weight loss and reduced appetite, the team identified 7,823 consumers who reported at least one symptom that could be medically classified.

It has been revealed that "A researcher might be able to examine a few thousand Reddit posts by hand, but looking at nearly 150,000 would be an enormous undertaking," says Sehgal. "AI makes it possible to analyze these conversations at scale, identifying patterns in what people are sharing that would otherwise be difficult to recognize.".

A Surprising Appetite Paradox Emerges.

The most striking difference involved hunger.

According to recent reports, in retatrutide's Phase 2 clinical trials (the drug is currently in Phase 3 trials, the final step before FDA approval), participants most commonly experienced gastrointestinal complaints, including nausea. These effects are familiar concerns with medications that influence appetite and digestion.

But among Reddit consumers who reported taking unapproved retatrutide, the pattern looked different. Increased appetite emerged as the most frequently described classifiable symptom, despite the substantial weight-loss effects demonstrated in clinical testing.

The researchers also compared the upcoming findings with their earlier analysis of semaglutide and tirzepatide.

According to recent reports, compared with those earlier Reddit reports, discussions involving unapproved retatrutide contained proportionally more mentions of appetite-related changes, sleep disturbances, increased heart rate, and muscle-related symptoms. Reports of nausea and other digestive complaints were proportionally less common.

Sources indicate that these differences could reflect how retatrutide interacts with the body. However, they could also result from differences between the groups of people discussing the medications, their other drug use, or the contents of the unapproved products.

"Retatrutide works differently from existing GLP-1 drugs, so it's possible that its effects on the body are different, too," notes Jena Shaw Tronieri, Senior Research Investigator at Penn's Center for Weight and Eating Disorders and a co-author of the study.

Recent findings suggest that "But the people discussing it on Reddit also may be different," she notes. "Users willing to obtain an unapproved medication on the gray market likely differ from other clinical populations. Some may be taking multiple experimental peptides, and we can't verify exactly what they're taking. We need more research to understand what, if anything, these differences in self-reported symptoms mean.".

Can AI Detect Drug Safety Concerns Earlier?

Beyond the findings about retatrutide, the study demonstrates how AI could potentially improve the early detection of drug safety concerns.

Industry observers note that traditional monitoring systems depend heavily on clinical trials, reports submitted to regulators, and information collected by healthcare professionals. People obtaining experimental medications through unapproved channels may not be represented in those systems.

Sources indicate that social media offers another source of information, allowing researchers to identify recurring experiences that might otherwise escape attention. However, these reports must be independently investigated before they can be considered reliable evidence of a drug-related problem.

The Penn team has already seen an example of how this approach can help guide further research.

In their previous investigation of semaglutide and tirzepatide, researchers identified online reports of menstrual irregularities. Those findings subsequently encouraged another scientific team to examine similar symptoms using the FDA's database of reported adverse drug events.

The follow-up study, published in Obstetrics & Gynecology, also detected disproportionate reports of certain menstrual changes. Although those findings did not establish causation, they provided additional reasons to investigate the potential connection.

The researchers hope their retatrutide findings will lead to similar independent studies, particularly as the drug advances through clinical development.

According to recent reports, "That's what we hope will happen with this study," claims Sehgal. "Other researchers can take what we find on Reddit and look for the same patterns in other datasets, using entirely different methods. Whether those signals hold up or not, the goal is to build a better understanding of what people are actually experiencing.".

The research was conducted through the University of Pennsylvania's School of Engineering and Applied Science and Perelman School of Medicine. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Weekly. Free. One click to leave.

Sources indicate that 7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

Recent findings suggest that every developer has shipped the other kind of page: a lovingly written article or landing page that peaks on launch day and then quietly rots. Screenshots age, statistics expire, rankings slide. Data-driven pages play the opposite game. Built from a living dataset, they republish themselves daily, grow to thousands of URLs, and answer questions nobody had asked when the site rolled out. This guide breaks down how they work, using a real fan-run stats site as the running example: one public dataset in, more than ten thousand fresh pages out.

Static pages lose ground because the web moves and they do not. Facts expire, competitors publish fresher answers, and search engines reward pages whose information matches today. A page that cannot revision itself must be rewritten by hand, so most sites update a few pages and abandon the rest.

Industry observers note that freshness is not one rule for the whole web; it depends on the query. Nobody needs a CSS tutorial rewritten weekly, but statistics, prices, availability and anything with a season attached decays on a schedule. Developers misjudge this constantly, treating every page like documentation when half their catalogue is really a perishable good. Serve a three-month-old stat as if it were current and readers learn the most damaging lesson a site can teach: do not trust the numbers here.

In a recent development, then there is the maintenance maths. A hundred hand-written pages each needing one review a year is a hundred small debts, and the interest compounds as the catalogue grows. The team updates the flagship pages, promises to return for the rest, and quietly never does. Data-driven architecture is really a staffing decision disguised as a technical one: humans design the system once, and the system does the updating forever.

A data-driven site has three layers: a dataset that refreshes on a schedule, templates that turn records into pages, and URL patterns that map every meaningful combination owners might search for. Change the data and every page changes; improve a template and ten thousand pages improve at once.

Recent findings suggest that the running example makes this concrete. A fan-built Overwatch stats tracker republishes Blizzard's public hero data on a daily cycle. From that one feed it generates hero profiles, head-to-head matchup pages and multi-condition tier lists: 10,291 URLs in its sitemap, across six languages, with matchup pages alone accounting for 8,586 of them. Nobody wrote those pages. Somebody designed the system that writes them, which is a very different, and much more scalable, job.

Recent findings suggest that the example runs on Next.js behind a CDN, but the stack is the least important layer of the three. The same pipeline feeding WordPress, Astro or a static site generator would look identical from the reader's side of the glass. Choose boring technology you already know, and spend your originality budget on the dataset and the templates, because that is where readers will feel the difference.

According to recent reports, generated pages stay useful when every URL must earn its existence with data. Set minimum thresholds before a page is published, give each template unique modules its siblings do not have, and noindex combinations with nothing to say. The line between a resource and spam is not automation; it is emptiness.

Sources indicate that quality gates work best when they are public and mechanical. The example site publishes its tier formula openly: 70% of the score from win rate, 30% from pick rate, and a hard floor that excludes heroes picked in under 0.5% of matches from topping the ranking, because a tiny sample cannot prove anything. That single floor is editorial policy expressed as code. Your version might be a minimum number of data points, a minimum price history, or a minimum review count — the number matters less than the fact that the gate exists and applies to every page equally.

Each template also needs modules its siblings cannot copy. A hero profile carries a seven-day trend and its best and worst matchups; a matchup page carries the head-to-head history; a tier list carries the movement since yesterday. Add a short human layer on top — a methodology page explaining the scoring, changelogs narrating what moved — and the catalogue stops reading as output and starts reading as a publication. Google's scaled-content rules target pages manufactured to manipulate rankings with little value; a page that answers a real query with real, current data is the opposite of that. The honest test for any generated URL is simple: if it vanished tonight, would a searcher lose an answer?

Start embarrassingly small: one dataset, one entity type, one template. A football club's results archive, a property portal's sold prices, your own product catalogue — anything structured and refreshed beats a grand strategy. Prove one template earns traffic, then add combinations, languages and dashboards in that order.

It has been revealed that what is programmatic SEO? Programmatic SEO means generating many pages from a structured dataset using templates, instead of writing each page by hand. Done well, each page answers a distinct search with real data. Done badly, it produces thousands of near-identical pages, which is where its reputation suffers.

Is programmatic SEO against Google's rules? No. Google's spam policies target scaled content created mainly to manipulate rankings, with little or no value for users. Pages generated from real data that answer real queries are publishing. The deciding question is whether a page helps its reader, not how it was produced.

It has been revealed that how often should the data behind pages refresh? Match the refresh to how fast the underlying facts change. Sports and game statistics justify daily pulls, prices often need hourly checks, and reference data may only move monthly. Refreshing faster than reality changes wastes crawl budget and makes 'updated' stamps meaningless.

Do generated pages need unique written text? They need unique value, which is not the same thing. Identical paragraphs on ten thousand pages add nothing, but unique data, comparisons and trends are content in their own right. Add short human-written context per template, and let the data carry the differences between pages.

According to recent reports, how many pages should a first project launch with? Launch with the smallest set that proves the template: one entity type, a few hundred pages at most. Validate that search engines index them and users engage before adding combinations and languages. Scaling an unproven template just manufactures tomorrow's cleanup job at industrial size.

It has been revealed that the sites quietly winning the long game are not publishing more; they are publishing systems. One honest dataset, one well-built template and strict quality gates will outlast a hundred hand-written pages competing on freshness alone. Try it this week: take one dataset you already own, design a single template with four real modules, and ship fifty pages. Watch what the data does next.

#149497. Back to The Future: Evaluating AI Agents on Predicting Future Events

AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Back to The Future: Evaluating AI Agents on Predicting Future Events

📅 17 Jul 2025 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1864 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Most current AI benchmarks focus on answering questions about the past, either by testing models on existing knowledge (in a static manner, such as HLE or GPQA, or augmented, like BrowseComp or GAIA) or previously solved problems (like PaperBench, DABStep, or most coding evaluations).
  • According to recent reports, forecasting future events is a complex and holistic task: it requires sophisticated reasoning, synthesis, weighing probabilities and genuine understanding, rather than pattern matching against or searching existing information.
  • Beyond its inherent importance, this forecasting-based approach also solves many methodological problems faced by current evaluations and benchmarks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Most current AI benchmarks focus on answering questions about the past, either by testing models on existing knowledge (in a static manner, such as HLE or GPQA, or augmented, like BrowseComp or GAIA) or previously solved problems (like PaperBench, DABStep, or most coding evaluations). However, we believe that more valuable AI, and ultimately AGI, will be distinguished by its ability to use this past to forecast interesting aspects of the future, rather than merely reciting old facts.

According to recent reports, forecasting future events is a complex and holistic task: it requires sophisticated reasoning, synthesis, weighing probabilities and genuine understanding, rather than pattern matching against or searching existing information. Evaluating models on their ability to predict future outcomes, whether in science, economics, geopolitics, or technology tests the kind of intelligence that creates real-world value.

Beyond its inherent importance, this forecasting-based approach also solves many methodological problems faced by current evaluations and benchmarks. Traditional benchmarks that measure accuracy on fixed test sets are inevitably affected by possible data contamination, and without access to the full reproducible training pipeline of a model, it's hard to trust the results. The most serious evaluation efforts now keep their test sets completely private, creating a frustrating arms race between evaluators and potential "gaming the leaderboard" mechanics (Singh et al., 2025).

In a recent development, forecasting makes contamination impossible by design, as you can't train on data that doesn't yet exist! This creates a level playing field where success depends on reasoning capability rather than memorization.

Industry observers note that perhaps most importantly, predictions about the future are inherently verifiable. We can wait and see who was right, creating an objective, time-stamped measure of model performance.

According to recent reports, we therefore propose evaluating agents on their ability to predict future events (Ye et al., 2024; Karger et al., 2025). FutureBench draws from real-world prediction markets and emerging news to create interesting prediction tasks grounded in actual future outcomes. We collect events from platforms and live news coverages and manifold markets, filtering them to focus on emerging events worth predicting. Using an agent-based approach, we curate scenarios that require genuine reasoning rather than simple pattern matching. Think geopolitical developments, market movements, or technology adoption trends - events where informed analysis actually matters.

This is the obvious question, and it's at the heart of what makes this benchmark interesting! We believe the answer cannot be a simple “yes” or a “no”, as it mostly depends on the actual questions; there are always key caveats to consider. Humans constantly use their ability to weigh current information to predict future events. Aren't most career moves, relationship choices, or even business strategies essentially bets on future outcomes?

Recent findings suggest that some predictions involve irreducible uncertainty (Will it rain on December 17th, 2027 at noon?), but many don't. When a skilled analyst predicts a firm's quarterly earnings or a policy expert forecasts election outcomes, they're using available information to make informed decisions. This is precisely what we're asking AI agents to do with FutureBench! The task isn't to get agents to fortune-tell, but rather to synthesize information and reason under stronger uncertainty than most other benchmarks.

The agent's prediction quality directly reflects its ability to search relevant information, synthesize complex data, and reason about cause-and-effect relationships. These are precisely the capabilities we want to measure in real-world applications.

Tools like DeepResearch are already used for market analysis and strategic planning. The quality of information collection strongly correlates with decision-making effectiveness. FutureBench is inspired by this evaluation process and tries to compute agents’ quality with objective, verifiable outcomes.

Building a benchmark that tests real prediction capabilities requires a steady stream of meaningful questions. We've developed two complementary approaches that capture different types of future events:.

Our first approach uses AI to mine current events for prediction opportunities. We deploy a smolagents-based agent to scrape a few major news websites, analyze front-page articles, and generate prediction questions about their likely outcomes. The agent reads through and identifies interesting articles and formulates specific, time-bound questions from their content, for example "Will the Federal Reserve cut interest rates by at least 0.25% by July 1st, 2025?".

We guide this process with carefully crafted prompts that specify what makes a good prediction question—events that are meaningful, verifiable, and uncertain extraction time.

The agent typically generates 5 questions per scraping session, with a time horizon of a single week, meaning that we assume we’ll know the answer to the question after seven days. This gives us a natural pipeline of fresh evaluation material tied to real-world events.

Our second source draws from Polymarket. These questions come from a prediction market platform where real participants make forecasts about future events. We presently ingest around 8 questions per week.

It has been revealed that however, the raw data needs filtering. We apply strong filtering to remove general questions regarding temperature and some questions regarding the stock and crypto markets, which would otherwise be too numerous for practical use in our benchmark. In addition to this, polymarket questions have less constraints regarding the final “realization” time, the actual outcome of the event could be available only next month or by the end of the year. These are still very relevant questions, but the data collection of the outcome is more sparse.

Here's an example of what comes out of our question generation pipeline:.

According to recent reports, the next question is, what does this type of benchmark allow us to measure? The framework operates on three distinct levels, allowing us to isolate exactly what we're measuring:.

Level 1: Framework Comparison Keep the underlying LLMs and tools constant while varying frameworks. How does a LangChain-based agent compare to one built with CrewAI when both use GPT-4 and the same search tools? This isolates the impact of different agentic frameworks.

In a recent development, level 2: Tool Performance Fix the LLM and framework while comparing different implementations. Which search tool (for example Tavily, Google, Bing) leads to better predictions than other search engines, holding everything else constant? This reveals which tools actually provide value. How much value do tools bring in general with respect to models without tools?

Industry observers note that level 3: Model Capabilities Hold the framework and tools constant while testing different LLMs. Given access to the same set of tools, does DeepSeek-V3 use them as effectively as GPT-4? This measures pure reasoning ability. This systematic approach lets us understand exactly where performance gains and losses occur in the agent pipeline.

It has been revealed that the benchmark also serves as a robust test of instruction following. Agents must respect specific formatting requirements and generate actions that can be correctly parsed and executed. In practice, this often reveals where smaller language models struggle with complex multi-step reasoning.

🚀 Try it yourself! Explore the live leaderboard: FutureBench Interactive Leaderboard.

We use SmolAgents as a baseline agent framework for all the questions. We also compute performance on the base models. For the prediction task itself, the agents get access to a focused toolkit:.

This intentionally lean setup forces agents to be strategic about information gathering while still providing the tools needed for informed predictions.

We compare different models using smolagents as a baseline (you can find the leaderboard on our HF Space). We also run the standard language models without internet access to estimate a general prior. As expected, we see agentic models performing better than simple language models; stronger models show more stable prediction quality. Overall we also find interesting patterns in how different models try to approach a question:.

Industry observers note that running this benchmark has revealed insights into how different models approach information gathering. One striking difference is with respect to scraping. GPT-4.1 appears to rely more on search results. Claude3.7 and 4 explore the web space in more detail and tend to use web scraping more frequently; this thorough approach also means collecting many more input tokens during the research process, thus increasing the cost.

Models show interesting approaches to making predictions, for example, to answer the question "Will annual inflation increase by 2.6 or more in June?":.

The DeepSeekV3 agent analyzed June 2025 inflation prospects by searching recent CPI data (finding current inflation at 2.4-2.8%), considered tariff impacts as upward pressure, and concluded inflation would exceed the 2.6% threshold.

Claude3.7 analyzed June 2025 inflation through comprehensive research (11 searches vs DeepSeekV3's 3), systematically gathering May 2025 CPI data (2.4% year-over-year), identifying decelerating monthly trends (0.2%→0.1%), weighing tariff pressures against Fed restrictive policy, calculating precise 0.2% gap needed, and concluded recent deceleration made reaching 2.6% threshold unlikely, answering "No.".

GPT4.1 analyzed June 2025 inflation through targeted searches for market consensus and forecasts, identified May 2025 CPI at 2.4% (below 2.5% expectations), noted weak 0.1% monthly increases, found no forecaster predictions of 2.6%+ for June, and concluded the jump from 2.4% to 2.6% was unlikely given recent below-expectation trends.

Interestingly, Claude was the only model that tried to access the Bureau of Labor Statistics website to scrape it directly, which failed because it is a .gov website and we do not allow this type of action.

The models exhibit distinct reasoning patterns in their outputs. GPT's analysis focused on consensus forecasts as the key signal for future events rather than extrapolating from current data, while Claude's approach exhibited rigorous analytical structure with its systematic pro/con framework and quantitative gap analysis, and DeepSeekV3's output displayed explicit acknowledgment of data limitations and systematic methodology adjustments when initial approaches encountered constraints.

Sources indicate that these behavioral differences reveal interesting patterns in how different models approach information gathering. The variations in web usage and token consumption suggest that models have distinct strategies for tackling prediction tasks, which FutureBench can help us measure and understand.

One challenge is that evaluation can be expensive due to the large number of input tokens. For example, Claude tends to visit web pages frequently, thus accumulating many input tokens. In a multi-turn loop, this can make the number of input tokens skyrocket very quickly. This increases the cost of any subsequent generation, even though most tokens are eventually cached.

It has been revealed that futureBench is an evolving benchmark, as we discover new findings and better patterns, we’ll keep incorporating them. We would love feedback from the community to understand how to better source questions, which experiments to run and which data is the most interesting to analyze.

YouTuber Charlotte Dobre would make YouTube commenters use their real names, if she had the power to implement a new rule on the platform.

There has been plenty of debate online over the years about whether or not people should be allowed to use personas and fake names to make comments on social media.

It has been revealed that like everywhere else, YouTube gives you the option to use your real name or a pseudonym, with plenty of people opting to reveal their true identities. They don’t always leave comments, so it makes things easier on that front.

Speaking to Dexerto, YouTuber and podcast host Charlotte Dobre revealed that, if she had the power to add a latest rule to YouTube, it would be to force people to expose their true identities when leaving comments.

Sources indicate that “Some people aren’t going to like this; I think that you should have to use your real name to comment. Everybody’s very brave behind a keyboard, but I’m curious how mean people would be if their real name was attached to it,” Dobre, who has just launched a pilot for her show Textuationships, stated.

Industry observers note that “I think people are emboldened by the fact that there are no repercussions for the stuff they say. Like, everything I say, there are repercussions for. I have to be so, so careful with what I say.

“I do think if there were consequences, ergo, like your name was attached to it, people would be a lot more careful.”.

The YouTuber noted that people have gotten angry at her in the comments over some of the advice she’s given out, especially when they believe she hasn’t given the ‘right’ advice.

YouTube will let other creators react live to your videos and keep the live ad revenue.

YouTubers will soon be able to strike down AI content impersonating them.

  • According to recent reports, by directing light onto either fin, the researchers can trigger muscle contractions that make the fin flap and push the robot through water.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A swimming robot does not necessarily need a bulky motor or powerful mechanical parts to move through water. MIT researchers have demonstrated that a single, carefully engineered layer of living muscle cells can generate enough force to propel a tiny robot forward.

Sources indicate that the engineers developed an extremely thin swimming robot that uses living muscle tissue to move its fins. Described in a new study published in Advanced Functional Materials, the device has a flexible gel framework roughly the length and width of a stick of gum. The gel forms two fins, each coated with a layer of muscle cells far thinner than a human hair. These cells have been genetically modified to contract when exposed to light.

According to recent reports, by directing light onto either fin, the researchers can trigger muscle contractions that make the fin flap and push the robot through water. Adjusting which fin receives light and how frequently it is illuminated allows the team to control both its speed and direction.

It has been revealed that in experiments, the remarkably thin robot successfully swam and turned through a simple underwater maze. At maximum speed, it covered approximately four times its body length per minute. Although that is much slower than an Olympic swimmer, who can travel up to 65 body lengths per minute, it is comparable to the swimming pace of a cow shark moving leisurely through the ocean.

Sources indicate that "It takes a lot of force to move through water versus air," indicates study author Ritu Raman, associate professor of mechanical engineering at MIT. "The robot's quite strong, given its size. ".

A New Generation of Robots Powered by Living Muscle.

The device represents the first demonstration of a very thin, two-dimensional robot that can move from place to place using living muscle tissue.

Most existing biohybrid robots rely on relatively large, three-dimensional structures made from laboratory-grown skeletal muscle. Producing these structures typically requires millions of cells. Raman explains that thinner designs could reduce manufacturing costs while potentially improving movement efficiency.

"At the moment, biohybrid robots from our group and others' are built from bulky, 3D chunks of lab-grown skeletal muscle that require millions of cells to fabricate," indicates Raman, who notes that thinner, less bulky designs such as the team's latest bot could be cheaper to build and could move more efficiently. "We believe that biohybrid robots powered by living muscle could one day perform delicate jobs like exploring environments too fragile or unpredictable for conventional hardware, because living tissue is soft, responsive to its surroundings, and can heal itself.".

The MIT research team also included first author Maheera Bawa, along with Arielle Berman, Laura Schwendeman, Ferdows Afghah, and Seanbiron Johnson.

From Artificial Muscle to a Swimming Robot.

In a recent development, the upcoming swimming robot builds on an earlier achievement by Raman's laboratory. Last year, the researchers created an artificial muscle disk inspired by the human iris, demonstrating how a thin layer of living cells could produce precisely controlled movements.

For that project, the engineers patterned a gel disk with grooves extending outward from its center and forming concentric circles. They then placed living muscle cells on the surface, where the cells grew into a thin layer following the patterned channels.

According to recent reports, when illuminated, the muscle tissue contracted in different directions, causing the disk to stretch and compress. Its movements resembled the way the iris of the human eye changes shape as the pupil expands or narrows.

The experiment established that researchers could grow extremely thin muscle layers in intricate arrangements and use light to control their movements along multiple directions.

"People hadn't seen this muscle architecture engineered from scratch before," Raman says. "And the cells were moving in multiple directions. But they only moved about 100 microns. From a robotics perspective, their movements were tiny.".

For the latest project, the researchers wanted to dramatically increase the amount of movement and force generated by the muscle cells. Their goal was to produce contractions powerful enough to propel a robot through water.

They determined that achieving this would require a better foundation for the living muscle tissue.

Recent findings suggest that the earlier artificial iris had used fibrin, an exceptionally soft gel, as its underlying structure. However, the team found that fibrin could swiftly shrink under the forces exerted by contracting muscle cells, limiting the effectiveness of the resulting movement.

To overcome this problem, the engineers investigated three characteristics of the gel foundation: its chemical composition, its stiffness, and the dimensions and geometry of the grooves used to organize muscle growth.

Sources indicate that "For engineering any type of tissue, it's known that these are knobs you can tune," Raman indicates. "And we wanted to optimize all these parameters to support live muscle cells.".

Engineering a Stronger Muscle-Powered Robot.

Finding the right supporting material required testing gels with different formulations, stiffness levels, and surface patterns.

The researchers compared several groove shapes, including narrow channels with square profiles and longer channels with curved bottoms. They discovered that muscle cells aligned more effectively inside square-shaped grooves.

This alignment was important because muscle cells that grow in the same direction are more likely to merge into fibers. Those fibers can then form stronger muscle tissue that contracts in a coordinated way. The square grooves therefore provided a more effective structure for producing force.

The team also replaced fibrin with gelatin methacrylate (GelMA), a material commonly used to grow and engineer biological tissue.

Industry observers note that by adjusting the formulation of GelMA, the researchers produced supporting gels with varying degrees of stiffness. They then examined how muscle cells developed on each surface and measured their ability to generate force.

Stiffer gels produced the best results. On these firmer surfaces, muscle cells grew in better alignment and generated stronger contractions.

Industry observers note that the engineers next investigated how thick the gel should be. They determined that a film measuring approximately half a millimeter offered an effective balance. It was sturdy enough to support a single layer of muscle cells while remaining sufficiently lightweight to prevent the contracting cells from detaching from the surface.

Industry observers note that the team further improved muscle performance through a form of exercise. Repeated pulses of light stimulated the cells to contract, strengthening the muscle tissue before it was incorporated into the swimming robot.

How Light Makes the Living Robot Swim.

With the gel structure optimized and the muscle cells strengthened, the researchers assembled their swimming device.

The finished robot consisted of a thin gel framework divided into two fins. Both sides of the gel were patterned with square-bottomed grooves and covered with living muscle cells. As the cells developed, they fused into organized muscle fibers capable of contracting together.

Each fin could be activated independently using light, giving the researchers a simple way to control the robot's movements.

"You can think of the robot as having two independent muscles," Raman says. "If we shine a light on just one, only that muscle moves. If shining on both, they both flap.".

It has been revealed that to test the device, the researchers placed it inside a large petri dish filled with water. They then moved a light source by hand, illuminating the fins to guide the robot through a maze positioned inside the dish.

Recent findings suggest that as the muscles contracted, the fins flapped and propelled the robot through the water. By changing the light stimulation, the engineers successfully controlled its movement and helped it navigate the obstacles.

Although the robot demonstrated the ability to swim and steer, its current shape remains relatively simple. The primary objective of the experiment was to establish that an exceptionally thin layer of engineered muscle tissue could generate enough force for swimming.

The researchers now strategy to refine the robot's body to improve its speed. Beyond demonstrating a new approach to biohybrid robotics, the technology could eventually be useful for monitoring aquatic environments or operating in locations where conventional rigid machines might cause damage.

"Our next goal is to optimize the body design to enable faster swimming," Raman states. "But even at slow swim speeds, one could imagine a muscle-powered swimmer being used for purposes like environmental monitoring in aquatic environments.".

Consilium: When Multiple LLMs Collaborate

📅 17 Jul 2025 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1212 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Picture this: four AI experts sitting around a poker table, debating your toughest decisions in real-time.
  • The platform works both as a visual Gradio interface and as an MCP (Model Context Protocol) server that integrates directly with applications like Cline (Claude Desktop had issues as the timeout could not be adjusted).
  • This wasn't my original hackathon idea.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Picture this: four AI experts sitting around a poker table, debating your toughest decisions in real-time. That's exactly what Consilium, the multi-LLM platform I built during the Gradio Agents & MCP Hackathon, does. It lets AI models discuss complex questions and reach consensus through structured debate.

The platform works both as a visual Gradio interface and as an MCP (Model Context Protocol) server that integrates directly with applications like Cline (Claude Desktop had issues as the timeout could not be adjusted). The core idea was always about LLMs reaching consensus through discussion; that's where the name Consilium came from. Later, other decision modes like majority voting and ranked choice were added to make the collaboration more sophisticated.

This wasn't my original hackathon idea. I initially wanted to build a simple MCP server to talk to my projects in RevenueCat. But I reconsidered when I realized a multi-LLM platform where these models discuss questions and return well-reasoned answers would be far more compelling.

The timing turned out to be perfect. Shortly after the hackathon, Microsoft published their AI Diagnostic Orchestrator (MAI-DxO), which is essentially an AI doctor panel with different roles like "Dr. Challenger Agent" that iteratively diagnose patients. In their setup with OpenAI o3, they correctly solved 85.5% of medical diagnosis benchmark cases, while practicing physicians achieved only 20% accuracy. This validates exactly what Consilium demonstrates: multiple AI perspectives collaborating can dramatically outperform individual analysis.

It has been revealed that after settling on the concept, I needed something that worked as both an MCP server and an engaging Hugging Face space demo. Initially I considered using the standard Gradio Chat component, but I wanted my submission to stand out. The idea was to seat LLMs around a table in a boardroom with speech bubbles, which should capture the collaborative discussion while also making it visually engaging. As I did not manage to style a standard table nicely so it was actually recognized as a table, I went for a poker-style roundtable. This approach also let me submit to two hackathon tracks by building a custom Gradio component and MCP server.

The custom Gradio component became the heart of the submission; the poker-style roundtable where participants sit and display speech bubbles showing their responses, thinking status, and research activities immediately caught the eye of anyone visiting the space. The component development was remarkably smooth thanks to Gradio's excellent developer experience, though I did encounter one documentation gap around PyPI publishing that led to my first contribution to the Gradio project.

The visual design proved robust throughout the hackathon; after the initial implementation, only features like user-defined avatars and center table text were added, while the core interaction model remained unchanged.

If you are interested in creating your own custom Gradio component you should take a look at Custom Components in 5 minutes and yes the title does not lie; it literally only takes 5 minutes for the basic setup.

Recent findings suggest that the visual roundtable maintains state through a session-based dictionary system where each user gets isolated state storage via user_sessions[session_id]. The core state object tracks participants, messages, currentSpeaker, thinking, and showBubbles arrays that are updated through update_visual_state() callbacks. When models are thinking, speaking, or research is being executed, the engine pushes incremental state updates to the frontend by appending to the messages array and toggling speaker/thinking states, creating the real-time visual flow without complex state machines - just direct JSON state mutations synchronized between backend processing and frontend rendering.

Industry observers note that while implementing, I realized there was no real discussion happening between the LLMs because they lacked clear roles. They received the full context of ongoing discussions but didn't know how to engage meaningfully. I introduced distinct roles to create productive debate dynamics, which, after a few tweaks, ended up being like this:.

In a recent development, this solved the discussion problem but raised a newly introduced question: how to determine consensus or identify the strongest argument? I implemented a lead analyst system where customers select one LLM to synthesize the final result and evaluate whether consensus was reached.

I also wanted consumers to control communication structure. Beyond the default full-context sharing, I added two alternative modes:.

In a recent development, finally, discussions need endpoints. I implemented configurable rounds (1-5), with testing showing that more rounds increase the likelihood of reaching consensus (though at higher computational cost).

Industry observers note that the current model selection includes Mistral Large, DeepSeek-R1, Meta-Llama-3.3-70B, and QwQ-32B. While notable models like Claude Sonnet and OpenAI's o3 are absent, this reflected hackathon credit availability and sponsor award considerations rather than technical limitations.

For models supporting function calling, I integrated a dedicated research agent that appears as another roundtable participant. Rather than giving models direct web access, this agent approach provides visual clarity about external resource availability and ensures consistent access across all function-calling models.

In a recent development, the research agent accesses five sources: Web Search, Wikipedia, arXiv, GitHub, and SEC EDGAR. I built these tools on an extensible base class architecture for future expansion while focusing on freely embeddable resources.

Since research operations can be time-intensive, the speech bubbles display progress indicators and time estimates to maintain user engagement during longer research tasks.

After the hackathon, Deborah Dahl introduced me to the Open Floor Protocol, which aligns perfectly with the roundtable approach. This protocol provides standardized JSON message formatting for cross-platform agent communication. Its key differentiator from other agent-to-agent protocols is that all agents maintain constant conversation awareness exactly like sitting at the same table. Another feature I have not seen with other protocols is that the floor manager can dynamically invite and remove agents from the floor and agents.

The protocol's interaction patterns map directly to Consilium's architecture:.

I'm at the moment integrating Open Floor Protocol support to allow users to add any OFP-compliant agents to their roundtable discussions. You can follow this development at: https://huggingface.co/spaces/azettl/consilium_ofp.

The hackathon introduced me to multi-agent debate research I hadn't previously encountered, including foundational studies like Encouraging Divergent Thinking in Large Language Models through Multi-Agent Debate. The community experience was remarkable; all participants actively supported each other through Discord feedback and collaboration. Seeing my roundtable component integrated into another hackathon project was one of my highlights working on Consilium.

I will continue to work on Consilium and with expanded model selection, Open Floor Protocol integration, and configurable agent roles, the platform could support virtually any multi-agent debate scenario imaginable.

Sources indicate that building Consilium reinforced my conviction that AI's future lies not just in more powerful individual models but in systems enabling effective AI collaboration. As specialized smaller language models become more efficient and resource-friendly, I believe roundtables of task-specific SLMs with dedicated research agents may provide compelling alternatives to general-purpose large language models for many use cases.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Nvidia has reinstated Jensen Huang as President and CEO after its Board of Directors unanimously voted to bring him back despite an ongoing investigation into national security concerns.
  • Huang had been temporarily replaced by Nvidia Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress following reports that the executive had been targeted by a foreign intelligence effort.
  • On November 23, Nvidia announced that Huang would return to his leadership positions effective immediately following a series of meetings with the board and consultations with senior US government officials.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nvidia has reinstated Jensen Huang as President and CEO after its Board of Directors unanimously voted to bring him back despite an ongoing investigation into national security concerns.

Huang had been temporarily replaced by Nvidia Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress following reports that the executive had been targeted by a foreign intelligence effort. The reports prompted the company’s board to establish an independent committee and retain outside legal counsel to investigate the matter.

On November 23, Nvidia announced that Huang would return to his leadership positions effective immediately following a series of meetings with the board and consultations with senior US government officials.

The controversy began in late October when The New York Times reported that Huang had a close relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based cloud computing firm Megaspeed whom US intelligence officials suspected of working for Chinese intelligence.

According to recent reports, megaspeed has also faced scrutiny over allegations that it helped Chinese companies obtain advanced Nvidia AI chips subject to US export restrictions. The Chinese government has denied the espionage allegations.

According to recent reports, on November 8, Huang admitted in a message to Nvidia employees that he had been unfaithful to his wife. Nvidia announced its independent investigation that same day.

NVIDIA Board reinstates Jensen Huang as President, CEO and Board Director.Read the release: https://t.co/x4bnjiSVil.

In a recent development, further reporting alleged that Huang had also engaged in an extramarital affair with Nvidia Vice President of Healthcare Kimberly Powell. On November 12, the manufacturer announced his resignation, ending his 33-year tenure as CEO.

However, less than two weeks later, Nvidia’s board reversed course, saying it was confident that Huang’s reinstatement posed no national security risk.

Sources indicate that “The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers,” Board Chair Harvey C. Jones said.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigns amid spy controversy.

Nvidia releases independent investigation into CEO after reports of suspected Chinese spy link.

Nvidia CEO warns US of dangers surrounding Chinese chip war.

“I am honored to return to NVIDIA and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a latest industrial revolution,” Huang said.

“I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment.”.

Despite his return, Nvidia confirmed that its independent investigation remains ongoing and that Huang has committed to cooperating with it.

The company has also established a National Security and Export Control Committee to oversee trade compliance and national security risks. Nvidia is additionally searching for a Chief Compliance Officer and will continue cooperating with government investigations.

  • Setting up WireGuard on a small virtual server is a satisfying infrastructure task.
  • The real engineering work starts when the team changes.
