📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that quantum physics places fundamental limits on what scientists can know about the behavior of particles. Werner Heisenberg's famous uncertainty principle states that certain properties, such as a particle's position and momentum, cannot both be measured with unlimited precision. This restriction is not caused by flaws in scientific instruments. It is built into the laws of nature.

But position and time are different. Heisenberg's uncertainty principle does not impose the same restriction on these quantities. Now, researchers have experimentally demonstrated another fundamental limitation: an electron's location and its behavior over time cannot both be determined with arbitrary precision. Known as the "space-time limit," this newly observed relationship could have major implications for the future of quantum technology and ultrafast electronics.

Industry observers note that the discovery comes from an international collaboration involving research groups at the Regensburg Center for Ultrafast Nanoscopy (RUN), led by Profs. Jascha Repp, Rupert Huber, Franz Giessibl, and Klaus Richter, along with a team at the Max Planck Institute in Hamburg led by Angel Rubio.

Watching Electrons Move at Incredible Speeds.

Industry observers note that understanding how matter behaves at the smallest scales is essential for developing the next generation of technology. Advances in clean energy, quantum computing, and powerful electronics for artificial intelligence all depend on knowing how chemical reactions unfold, how light interacts with materials, and how electrons travel through electronic devices.

In a recent development, however, even the sharpest microscopic photographs cannot reveal the full picture. Scientists also need to observe how these processes change over time, effectively creating slow-motion movies of events occurring at the atomic scale.

At RUN, researchers are developing ultrafast microscopes capable of recording the movements of electrons, atoms, and molecules with extraordinary precision in both space and time. About ten years ago, scientists in Regensburg used ultrafast scanning tunneling microscopy to resolve the movement of a single molecule across space and time for the first time.

Tracking individual electrons presents an even greater challenge. At these microscopic distances, electrons can move roughly a thousand times faster than atoms and molecules, with important changes taking place over just attoseconds.

Industry observers note that to appreciate how extreme these scales are, consider that an atom is approximately ten million times smaller than a millimeter. An attosecond is one-billionth of a billionth of a second. The difference between an attosecond and a second is comparable to the difference between one second and the entire age of the universe.

Sources indicate that making these measurements is especially difficult because electrons do not behave like ordinary objects. Their motion follows the unusual laws of quantum mechanics rather than the familiar rules of classical physics.

Ultrafast Lasers Reveal Quantum Tunneling.

To observe electron behavior at these extraordinary speeds, the researchers built a latest laser system that provides much finer time resolution than earlier experiments. The system allows them to control and study the quantum motion of individual electrons directly.

In the experiments, carefully timed laser pulses drive electrons from an extremely sharp metal tip toward a silver surface. The distance they travel is only a few atomic diameters.

Industry observers note that the researchers detect this movement by measuring the resulting electrical current. To determine exactly when the electrons move, they use two pulses of light separated by a precisely controlled interval.

Simon Maier, the lead author of the paper, explains: "By varying the time interval between the two laser pulses, we can directly observe how the electrons respond.".

It has been revealed that this approach revealed clear evidence of electron motion occurring on attosecond timescales. It highlighted that the laser pulses could transfer electrons within these incredibly brief intervals while allowing scientists to observe the process as it happened.

What makes the result particularly remarkable is how the electrons travel. Instead of moving like conventional particles, they behave as quantum waves. This allows them to pass through an energy barrier separating the metal tip from the silver surface, even though classical physics predicts they should not have enough energy to cross it.

This phenomenon, known as quantum tunneling, is somewhat like an object passing through a solid wall without breaking or damaging it.

"Our measurement can be understood as a high-speed camera for the electron wave packets, since you can see at what point in time the tunneling process takes place," explains Katharina Glöckl, a doctoral student and co-author of the publication.

A Surprising 500-Attosecond Delay.

Recent findings suggest that to understand the measurements more deeply, researchers working with Prof. Angel Rubio performed sophisticated quantum simulations of the electrons' behavior near the "space-time limit.".

In a recent development, their calculations closely reproduced the experimental findings and uncovered another remarkable detail. The electrons did not respond to the light field instantaneously. Instead, their motion lagged behind it by approximately 500 attoseconds.

At such extreme scales, several fundamental features of quantum physics become vital simultaneously.

According to recent reports, for example, the researchers found that the laser pulses could not be described entirely by treating light as a wave or entirely by treating it as individual particles called photons. Their effects displayed characteristics of both descriptions. This combination was essential for exploring electron behavior so close to the "space-time limit.".

The team also discovered that controlling electron motion over extremely short intervals changes how the electrons are distributed in space. Quantum mechanics describes these electrons using wave packets, which represent how their wave properties extend across different locations.

The relationship between the timing of electron motion and the spatial extent of these wave packets revealed the central limitation behind the discovery.

A Hidden Tradeoff Between Space and Time.

Raffael Spachtholz, another co-author of the study, explains: "The more precisely we want to pin down the electron's position in time, the more energy we need to provide. And as a result, the electron wave packet spreads out more spatially.".

According to recent reports, in other words, improving the precision of an electron's timing comes with a cost. The more tightly researchers define when its motion occurs, the more broadly its quantum wave packet spreads through space.

To examine this relationship experimentally, the team placed a single atom on the surface to confine the electron wave packets to an extremely small region immediately before the laser pulses arrived.

This setup allowed the scientists to directly measure the connection between the electrons' spatial distribution and the timing of their motion.

Importantly, even when the electrons received substantial energy from the laser pulses, their wave packets remained sufficiently localized for microscopy with atomic spatial resolution and attosecond time resolution.

The findings provide experimental insight into a fundamental space-time constraint that scientists had previously only suspected. They also make it possible to systematically investigate how changes in electron motion over time affect the spatial structure of quantum wave functions.

Could Quantum Electronics Become Hundreds of Thousands of Times Faster?

Beyond revealing a fresh aspect of quantum behavior, the discovery could open the door to technologies that operate on timescales far beyond the capabilities of today's electronics.

One especially promising possibility involves using precisely controlled electron wave packets to influence chemical reactions.

Transferring a single electron to a molecule represents the smallest possible transfer of electric charge. But when that electron is concentrated within an exceptionally small region of space and time, the resulting local peak current density can reach as much as 1 trillion amperes per square centimeter.

Such extreme conditions could give scientists latest ways to control chemical bonds and observe how molecules change during reactions.

It has been revealed that "In the future, we want to use such wave packets to specifically trigger chemical reactions and observe, on the relevant length and time scales, how chemical bonds can be broken or altered," explains Prof. Jascha Repp enthusiastically.

In a recent development, the implications could extend well beyond chemistry. Greater control over electron motion may eventually help engineers develop electronic devices and quantum information systems that operate at speeds approaching the fundamental limits of electron dynamics.

It has been revealed that "In the long term, the insights gained could also contribute to operating electronics and quantum information processing at the intrinsic speed limit of electron motion itself -- hundreds of thousands of times faster than the presently dominant CMOS technology," adds Prof. Rupert Huber.

That possibility remains a long term technological goal rather than an achievement demonstrated in the current experiments. Nevertheless, the findings provide a fresh foundation for exploring how electrons can be manipulated at the smallest distances and shortest timescales.

In a recent development, for Repp and Huber, the results suggest that the range of potential applications is extraordinarily broad. They believe that future advances in controlling electrons at the space-time limit may ultimately depend more on human creativity than on the constraints imposed by nature.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The owner of a dwindling empire of Wendy’s restaurants on Friday disclosed its looks to close several more stores, bringing its total number of shuttered locations to almost 100. It’s a grim milestone for the popular burger chain as it works to execute on a turnaround initiative aimed at boosting sales and bolstering its brand image. The franchisee behind the closures, Meritage Hospitality Group of Grand Rapids, Michigan, is among the largest operators within the Wendy’s system, at one time owning roughly 375 locations across 15 states. It closed dozens of those restaurants in the months before a Chapter 11 bankruptcy filing in September, and has since shuttered additional waves of stores at regular intervals as part of cash collateral agreements with its lenders. How many Wendy’s stores has Meritage closed? According to court documents, Meritage has closed well over 90 Wendy’s locations since late last year, with many of those stores shuttered before its September bankruptcy petition. As is typical in Chapter 11 cases, Meritage is seeking to reject the leases on many of the stores that it closed pre-bankruptcy—roughly 60, court filings show—a list that includes a handful of Taco John’s and Morning Belle locations, in addition to Wendy’s. Since the bankruptcy, Meritage has also closed at least 41 additional Wendy’s restaurants, including six closures that were disclosed on Friday. The newly shuttered restaurants were located in Florida, Georgia, Michigan, and Ohio: 12135 Lem Turner Road Jacksonville, FL 32218 1928 Hwy 155 McDonough, GA 30252 3675 Cascade Road Atlanta, GA 30331 9556 US 31 So Interlochen, MI 49643 8258 Broadmoor Avenue Caledonia, MI 49316 914 Conant St. Maumee, OH 43537 Prior to the above six restaurants, Meritage disclosed waves of store closures on at least five separate occasions: 5 locations on September 25 5 locations on October 2 10 locations on October 9 13 stores on October 16 2 stores on October 30 Fast Company has reached out to Meritage Hospitality Group and Wendy’s for comment. What will happen to Meritage’s remaining stores? Meritage has owned Wendy’s restaurants since the late 1990s, but its relationship with the fast food giant appeared to turn increasingly contentious in recent years as its business faced headwinds on numerous fronts—including due to the soaring cost of beef. The franchisee has also blamed Wendy’s for a strategy of “deep discounting” that it says squeezed profits. The Wendy’s Company, for its part, had sought to terminate Meritage’s franchise agreements, claiming to be owed more than $146 million in past-due royalties and other fees. Despite all this animosity, the two sides are working together to salvage what’s left of the Meritage fleet. Wendy’s disclosed earlier this month that it wants to buy up to 163 restaurants from Meritage. That deal, which is still subject to better bids, is expected to close early next year. Additionally, Meritage is moving to sell restaurants to various other buyers in separate deals, including one to sell 42 locations in Arkansas, Mississippi, Missouri, and Tennessee to an entity called Divine Infinity Operations. It’s unclear if additional Wendy’s locations could close before or after these asset sales are complete. This story is developing….

Stop your browser from killing your laptop battery with these 3 tweaks

💡 Key Takeaways

  • According to recent reports, you unplug your laptop with a full charge, sit down at a coffee shop to get some work done, and an hour later your battery is already at 50%.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that you unplug your laptop with a full charge, sit down at a coffee shop to get some work done, and an hour later your battery is already at 50%. You check your system settings to see what’s killing your power, and the culprit is exactly what you suspected: your web browser. Modern websites are effectively heavy software applications running constantly in the background. If you keep dozens of tabs open, your browser is caching media, running ad scripts, and refreshing data for every single one of them simultaneously. It eats up your system memory and forces your processor to work overtime. You don’t have to change the way you work or close your research tabs to get your battery life back. You just need to flip a few switches hidden in your browser’s settings menu. Turn on native memory savers Both Chrome and Edge finally have built-in tools to stop background tabs from draining power. In Chrome, go to Settings, click Performance and turn on Memory Saver and choose the Maximum option. In Edge, go to Settings, click System and Performance > Performance, and turn on Enable Energy Saver, then set it to Maximum Savings. Then toggle Automatically Put Tabs to Sleep on. This setting automatically puts inactive tabs to sleep until you click back to them. Stop background apps from running when closed By default, browsers like to keep their background processes running even after you’ve closed the browser window entirely. This is terrible for your battery. Go to Chrome’s Settings, click System, and toggle off the switch that notes “Continue running background apps when Google Chrome is closed.” In Edge, go to System and Performance > System and toggle off “Continue running background extensions and apps when Edge is closed.” Use a tab discarding extension If you’re someone who keeps fifty tabs open at all times, native memory savers might not be aggressive enough. Install a free extension such as Auto Tab Discard. It lets you set strict rules, like automatically unloading any tab you haven’t looked at in 10 minutes. The tab stays visible in your top bar, but it uses absolutely zero battery power until you click it again.

According to recent reports, you unplug your laptop with a full charge, sit down at a coffee shop to get some work done, and an hour later your battery is already at 50%. You check your system settings to see what’s killing your power, and the culprit is exactly what you suspected: your web browser.

Modern websites are effectively heavy software applications running constantly in the background. If you keep dozens of tabs open, your browser is caching media, running ad scripts, and refreshing data for every single one of them simultaneously. It eats up your system memory and forces your processor to work overtime.

According to recent reports, you don’t have to change the way you work or close your research tabs to get your battery life back. You just need to flip a few switches hidden in your browser’s settings menu.

Both Chrome and Edge finally have built-in tools to stop background tabs from draining power. In Chrome, go to Settings, click Performance and turn on Memory Saver and choose the Maximum option.

In Edge, go to Settings, click System and Performance > Performance, and turn on Enable Energy Saver, then set it to Maximum Savings.

Then toggle Automatically Put Tabs to Sleep on. This setting automatically puts inactive tabs to sleep until you click back to them.

By default, browsers like to keep their background processes running even after you’ve closed the browser window entirely. This is terrible for your battery.

Go to Chrome’s Settings, click System, and toggle off the switch that claims “Continue running background apps when Google Chrome is closed.”.

In Edge, go to System and Performance > System and toggle off “Continue running background extensions and apps when Edge is closed.”.

In a recent development, if you’re someone who keeps fifty tabs open at all times, native memory savers might not be aggressive enough. Install a free extension such as Auto Tab Discard.

In a recent development, it lets you set strict rules, like automatically unloading any tab you haven’t looked at in 10 minutes. The tab stays visible in your top bar, but it uses absolutely zero battery power until you click it again.

Breaking: Inside this quantum computer, memory vibrates like a guitar string

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1132 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that A quantum computer might seem to have little in common with a guitar, but researchers at ETH Zurich have found a surprising connection.
  • Unlike the sounds produced by a musical instrument, these vibrations occur at frequencies far beyond human hearing.
  • Industry observers note that by harnessing these vibrations, the researchers have created a way for quantum computers to process information efficiently while accessing a flexible working memory.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that A quantum computer might seem to have little in common with a guitar, but researchers at ETH Zurich have found a surprising connection. Physicist Yiwen Chu and her team have developed a system that uses microscopic mechanical vibrations to store and manipulate quantum information, much like the vibrating strings of a guitar produce musical notes.

Unlike the sounds produced by a musical instrument, these vibrations occur at frequencies far beyond human hearing. They take place within a tiny quantum chip, where they serve as a newly introduced form of computer memory.

Industry observers note that by harnessing these vibrations, the researchers have created a way for quantum computers to process information efficiently while accessing a flexible working memory. "The interaction between the quantum processor and the quantum memory provides a crucial foundation with a view to establishing quantum computers as a powerful and reliable way to perform computations that are not feasible with conventional computers," says Yiwen Chu.

Industry observers note that the breakthrough, described in the journal Science, introduces a different approach to quantum computer design. Instead of closely integrating information processing and storage, as many existing systems do, Chu's team has developed an architecture that gives these functions more distinct roles.

Quantum Memory Inspired by Conventional Computers.

The researchers drew inspiration from the basic design of everyday digital computers. In a conventional machine, the central processing unit (CPU) carries out calculations while information is held separately in working memory, commonly called random access memory (RAM). The arrangement of these components plays an important role in determining how efficiently a computer operates.

Chu's quantum system follows a similar principle. A superconducting qubit acts as the processing and control unit, performing a role comparable to that of the central processing unit (CPU). Meanwhile, a separate quantum memory temporarily holds the information needed during calculations, allowing the processor to retrieve and modify it as necessary.

The major difference lies in how that information is stored.

"In our quantum working memory, however, information is not stored electromagnetically -- as is usually the case today -- but rather in the form of mechanical vibrations," explains Chu.

Sources indicate that quantum computers take advantage of unusual properties of quantum physics, including superposition, which allows quantum systems to exist in combinations of different states, and entanglement, which creates powerful connections between quantum states. These effects could eventually enable quantum machines to tackle certain extremely complicated calculations much faster than conventional computers, including some problems that are currently beyond their practical capabilities.

Why Vibrating Quantum Memory Could Be Better.

One of the greatest challenges in quantum computing is maintaining precise control over quantum information. The states used for calculations are delicate, and even small disturbances can cause information to be lost. To perform calculations reliably, the processor and memory must interact closely enough to transfer and manipulate quantum states with high precision.

Recent findings suggest that in the latest system, microscopic structures called mechanical resonators hold information in particular patterns of vibration. When the superconducting qubit needs that information, it accesses the stored vibrational state, performs the required operation, and returns the modified information to memory.

Industry observers note that many existing quantum computers instead use electromagnetic memory alongside superconducting qubits. Researchers understand these technologies well, and they can be combined to provide extremely accurate control over quantum states, including reading, changing, and manipulating stored information.

However, electromagnetic memory systems have a significant disadvantage. They can occupy considerable space, making it difficult to expand experimental quantum devices into the larger, more capable computers that researchers and industries ultimately need.

Industry observers note that mechanical resonators offer several potential advantages. They are substantially smaller, allowing more compact designs. They can also support numerous different patterns of vibration, providing opportunities to store more information simultaneously than conventional electromagnetic memory.

Industry observers note that another important benefit is that mechanical vibrations can preserve quantum states for longer periods before the stored information begins to fade. Longer storage times could make it easier to carry out complicated calculations that require information to remain available throughout multiple processing steps.

Latest Quantum Computer Passes Major Tests.

The research published in Science provides the first experimental demonstration that mechanical resonators can work together with superconducting qubits to carry out quantum computations. The results establish that vibration-based memory is a feasible alternative to electromagnetic storage.

According to recent reports, the achievement goes beyond simply storing information. Chu's team demonstrated that its architecture can handle both relatively straightforward calculations and more demanding quantum operations.

In a recent development, to evaluate the system, the researchers tested two important computational techniques: the quantum Fourier transform and period finding. Both are fundamental tools in quantum computing and require a computer to coordinate multiple quantum states with considerable precision.

"The Quantum Fourier Transform is a fundamental computational procedure required for many quantum algorithms. The period-finding algorithm we implemented served as a demonstration of how this procedure can be used," explains Igor Kladaric, doctoral student in Chu's team and co-author of the publication.

Successfully completing these tasks requires the system to store, control, and maintain coherent relationships among multiple quantum states at the same time. The experiments showed that the newly introduced architecture can meet these requirements, providing strong evidence that it can support genuine quantum computation rather than simply function as a memory device.

A Promising Step Toward Powerful Quantum Computers.

Industry observers note that one of the most significant findings is that the upcoming system can, in principle, carry out all the fundamental operations needed for arbitrary quantum computations. This means the architecture has the essential capabilities required for a programmable, general-purpose quantum computer.

However, demonstrating those capabilities in an experimental chip is only the beginning. The next major challenge is scaling the technology to larger systems with greater processing power while preserving the precision and reliability demonstrated in the laboratory.

It has been revealed that chu and her colleagues are continuing to investigate how their approach can be developed further. Its long-term success will depend on whether mechanical quantum memory can remain effective as more components and increasingly complex computations are added.

Practical quantum computers powerful enough for widespread scientific and industrial applications are still some distance away. Nevertheless, by showing that tiny mechanical vibrations can serve as compact, capable quantum memory, the ETH Zurich team has demonstrated a promising new route toward making those machines a reality.

#149458. Industry News: 5 tips for an annual review to kick off 2027

Industry News: 5 tips for an annual review to kick off 2027

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (3011 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that below, Tiago Forte shares five key insights from his upcoming book, Life in Perspective: The Art and Power of the Annual Life Review.
  • Below, Tiago Forte shares five key insights from his new book, Life in Perspective: The Art and Power of the Annual Life Review.
  • Forte is a productivity expert and founder of Forte Labs, where he teaches people how to use technology to enhance their creativity and effectiveness.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that below, Tiago Forte shares five key insights from his upcoming book, Life in Perspective: The Art and Power of the Annual Life Review. Forte is a productivity expert and founder of Forte Labs, where he teaches people how to use technology to enhance their creativity and effectiveness. He is best known for developing the Building a Second Brain methodology. What’s the Major Idea? Most of us don’t get to choose our moments of clarity. They arrive by accident: a long flight, a chance conversation, a crisis that rearranges our priorities overnight. An annual review lets you create that clarity on purpose, once a year, for the rest of your life. Listen to the audio version of this Book Bite—read by Forte himself—in the Next Big Idea app, or buy the book. 1. Start with the past, not with goals. Every January, millions of people sit down with a blank page and ask, “What do I want this year?” They try to reinvent themselves on the spot, ignoring everything their own history says about what that would take. Before you set a single goal, spend a few hours looking back at the year you’ve lived: your calendar, the photos on your phone, your journal, the passages you highlighted. There are two reasons why this matters: Your memory is far less reliable than it feels. Every time you recall a memory, it gets subtly rewritten. And carrying a camera everywhere hasn’t fixed the problem. As Jason Farago wrote in The New York Times, we live in a time when “everything is recorded, nothing is remembered.” Your brain doesn’t have a separate system for imagining the future. Remembering and imagining run on the same core network. When you picture your future self, your brain is recombining fragments of your past into new scenarios. So the richer your picture of the past, the better your raw material for imagining what comes next. There’s a practical payoff too. Dig beneath most people’s goals, and you’ll find that what they really want is to feel a certain way: at peace, in control, proud of themselves. Instead of projecting that feeling onto some distant future, you can look back at the last time you felt it and study what made it possible. Your past is the most reliable evidence you have about what makes you come alive. Start there. 2. Stop giving yourself a performance review. When most of us look back on our year, we slip into the only mode of evaluation we know: judgment. We tally up where we fell short, catalog our failures, and hand down a verdict. It feels rigorous. The research says it backfires. In a Gallup study called More Harm Than Good, only 14% of employees strongly agreed that their performance reviews inspired them to improve. About a third of the time, reviews made performance worse. Critical feedback puts people on the defensive. If that’s what criticism does coming from a manager, imagine what it does coming from inside your own head. So use a different lens: appreciation. The word appreciate has two meanings. It means to recognize the value of something. It’s also what happens to an asset over time: It grows in value. What you appreciate appreciates. Ask “What went surprisingly well?” before you ask, “Why did I fail?” This also means your review should be enjoyable. Honest reflection will sometimes bring up hard emotions, and that’s fine. But if you find yourself dreading any part of it, that’s the number one warning sign you’ve gone off track. If journaling feels like pulling teeth, record voice memos on a walk instead. Spread your photos across the floor. Put on your favorite music. One of my students put it this way after trying this approach: “I’ve spent years treating my life as a list of problems to solve. But what if, instead of fixing myself, I changed how I see myself?” In a war with yourself, you always lose. 3. Complain and compare, on purpose. We’ve been told since childhood not to complain or compare ourselves to others. During your review, I suggest doing both deliberately. Start with complaining. Pick the area of life you’re least happy with and spend half an hour writing out every specific symptom. What exactly is wrong? What’s missing? What isn’t fair? Think of it like describing symptoms to a doctor. Hiding them only leads to the wrong diagnosis. Then comes the hard part: Resist the urge to fix anything yet. The moment you jump to solutions, your understanding crystallizes and your learning stops. You latch on to the first plausible fix. Instead, look at the whole list and ask what single source might be driving all of it. A dozen separate problems often trace back to one root cause, and you’ll never see it if you rush to treat each symptom one at a time. Now, comparison. The standard advice is to stop comparing yourself to others, and it has never really worked. Use those comparisons as data. Jealousy is one of the most honest emotions we have, precisely because we can’t control it. You don’t get to choose what provokes your envy. That means it’s pointing at a desire or a value you may not have admitted to yourself yet. So the next time someone’s post gives you a flash of envy, skip the shame and get curious. What exactly do they have that you want? Then bring yourself back to your own baseline. Swap “Am I successful?” for “Where have I succeeded?” Swap “Am I happy?” for “What am I happy about?” Your complaints show you what needs to change. Your envy demonstrates you what you want instead. 4. Let your emotions cast a vote. Most goal-setting advice speaks the language of the intellect: systems, objectives, strategy, discipline. Smart, capable people are especially prone to making prepares that make perfect sense logically and zero sense at the level of the heart. We’ve been taught that emotions cloud our judgment. But neuroscientist Antonio Damasio spent decades studying patients with damage to the emotional centers of their brains. Their logic was perfectly intact, yet they struggled to make even simple decisions, like what to eat for lunch or when to schedule an appointment. Without emotion, every option looked equally valid. Emotions are the foundation of good decisions. They’re your nervous system’s way of compressing a lifetime of experience into a signal you can feel before you can put it into words. So when you’re weighing a new direction or commitment for the year ahead, pay attention to your body. Look for “three signs of yes”: A quickening of your breath A flush of warmth in your face or chest A tingling at the back of your neck Goose bumps A catch in your throat Any one of these on its own could be nothing. When three or more show up together, your intuition is casting a vote. The opposite signal matters just as much. Notice the knot in your stomach when you think about a certain commitment, or the way some tasks keep getting pushed to next week, and the week after. That’s your internal “no.” You have to hear it before you can say it out loud. Don’t act on impulse, but give your intuition a seat at the table for the one ritual of the year designed to hear it. Your mind can rationalize anything. Your body tells the truth. 5. Strategy for the three-week wall. New Year’s resolutions have a bad reputation. But research by the psychologist John Norcross found that people who made formal resolutions were about 10 times more likely to succeed six months later than people with the same goals who didn’t. So setting the intention helps. The trouble starts a few weeks later. The most common mistake after a review is starting too many new things in the rush of fresh energy. Psychologist Brian Little found that the average person juggles about 15 active projects at a time. Once you count everything you’re already committed to, most people have room for two or three new ones at most. So before adding anything, go through your current commitments and decide what to cancel, pause, or hand off. And turn vague wishes into concrete projects. “Get healthier” has no beginning, no end, and no obvious next step. “Complete a 30-day walking challenge” does. Then expect the wall. About three weeks after a review, the daily grind reasserts itself, and the vision starts to fade at the edges. Fitness app Strava analyzed 800 million data points from its users and named January 19th “Quitters’ Day,” the day most people abandon their new exercise habit. The answer is structure. In one study, people who wrote down their goals and sent weekly progress updates to a friend achieved them at nearly twice the rate of those who only thought about them: 76% versus 43%. So share what you’re working toward with a few people you trust. And schedule check-ins: a short one each month, and a deeper one at the midpoint of the year. To have more inflection points in your life, you need more reflection points. This article originally appeared in Next Big Idea Club magazine and is reprinted with permission. 💡 Key Takeaways

  • If you have trained your own machine learning model, you know how vital it is to be able to track metrics, parameters, and hyperparameters during training and visualize them afterwards to better understand your training run.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

TL;DR: Trackio is a new, open-source, and free experiment tracking Python library that provides a local dashboard and seamless integration with Hugging Face Spaces for easy sharing and collaboration. Since trackio is a drop-in replacement for wandb, you can get started with the syntax you already know!

If you have trained your own machine learning model, you know how vital it is to be able to track metrics, parameters, and hyperparameters during training and visualize them afterwards to better understand your training run.

Industry observers note that most machine learning researchers use specific experiment tracking libraries to do this. However, these libraries can be paid, require complex setup, or lack the flexibility needed for rapid experimentation and sharing.

At Hugging Face, our science team has started using Trackio for our research projects, and we've found several key advantages over other tracking solutions:.

Sources indicate that easy Sharing and Embedding: Trackio makes it incredibly simple to share training progress with colleagues or embed plots directly in blog posts and documentation using iframes. This is especially valuable when you want to showcase specific training curves or metrics without requiring others to set up accounts or navigate complex dashboards.

Standardization and Transparency: Metrics like GPU energy usage are important to track and share with the community so we can have a better idea of the energy demands and environmental impacts of model training. Using Trackio, which directly gets information from the nvidia-smi command, makes it easy to quantify and compare energy usage and to add it to model cards.

According to recent reports, data Accessibility: Unlike some tracking tools that lock your data behind proprietary APIs, Trackio makes it straightforward to extract and analyze the data being recorded. This is crucial for researchers who need to perform custom analysis or integrate training metrics into their research workflows.

Flexibility for Experimentation: Trackio's lightweight design allows us to easily experiment with new tracking features during training runs. For instance, we can decide when to move tensors from GPU to CPU when logging tensors while training, which significantly improves training throughput when you need to track model/intermediate states without impacting performance.

Ok then, so what is Trackio and how do you use it? Trackio is an open-source Python library that lets you track any metrics and visualize them using a local Gradio dashboard. You can also sync this dashboard to Hugging Face Spaces, which means you can then share the dashboard with other consumers simply by sharing a URL. Since Spaces can be private or public, this means you can share a dashboard publicly or just within members of your Hugging Face organization.

You can install trackio using pip:.

According to recent reports, trackio is designed to be a drop-in replacement for experiment tracking libraries like wandb. The API is compatible with wandb.init, wandb.log, and wandb.finish, so you can simply import trackio as wandb in your code.

After logging your experiments, you can launch the dashboard to visualize your results. Run the following command in your terminal:.

You can also specify a project name:.

To sync your local dashboard to Hugging Face Spaces, simply pass a space_id to init:.

If you are hosting your dashboard on Spaces, you can simply share the URL or embed it anywhere using an iframe:.

Since Spaces can be private or public, this means you can share a dashboard publicly or just within members of your Hugging Face organization — all for free!

When you sync your Trackio dashboard to Hugging Face Spaces, the data is logged to an ephemeral Sqlite database on Spaces. Because this database is reset if your Space restarts, Trackio also converts the Sqlite database to a Parquet dataset and backs it up to a Hugging Face Dataset every 5 minutes. This means you can visualize your logged metrics in a Hugging Face dataset at any time easily:.

Tip: you can set the name of this dataset by passing in a dataset_id to trackio.init().

Trackio integrates natively with Hugging Face libraries like transformers and accelerate, so you can log metrics with minimal setup.

No extra setup needed—just plug it in and start tracking.

Trackio is intentionally lightweight and is right now in beta. Some features found in other tracking tools, such as artifact management, or complex visualizations, are not available yet. If you'd like to have these features, please create issues here: https://github.com/gradio-app/trackio/issues.

Given Trackio's lightweight and open-source nature, we'd love to work with the machine learning community to design an experiment tracking product that works for all of us!

Please let us know any features you'd like to see in Trackio here: https://github.com/gradio-app/trackio/concerns.

  • Sources indicate that despite being one of the richest people on Earth right now, Musk is relying on a financing deal to acquire the chips he needs to achieve his dream of building an AI LLM that will “assist in the pursuit of understanding.” The $43 billion “Project Saturn” loan is also not structured like a typical loan, so its investment-grade rating would remain unaffected.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that elon Musk is borrowing $43 billion to finance SpaceX's acquisition of Nvidia AI chips for its ambitious data center projects and is using the semiconductors as collateral. However, Ars Technica reports that lenders are concerned that SpaceX will use the chips for its planned orbital data center, making it difficult, if not impossible, for creditors to reclaim in case the firm defaults on its loan. SpaceX stated it will deploy the collateralized chips only on Earth, but it remains unclear whether this provision is included in the signed debt instrument.

SpaceX is working on building massive data centers on both Earth and in space. Musk has already revealed the organization’s first-generation AI1 satellite, with a 120-kilowatt payload and a span that’s larger than a Boeing 747, while he’s also planning to build a $24-billion gas-powered AI supercomputer in Starbase, Texas. These projects are in addition to the Colossus 1 and Colossus 2 sites near the Tennessee-Mississippi border.

Sources indicate that despite being one of the richest people on Earth right now, Musk is relying on a financing deal to acquire the chips he needs to achieve his dream of building an AI LLM that will “assist in the pursuit of understanding.” The $43 billion “Project Saturn” loan is also not structured like a typical loan, so its investment-grade rating would remain unaffected. Instead, it’s built similarly to aircraft leasing agreements, in which a leasing manufacturer buys the jets and leases them to the airline that wants to use them. This saves the airline from having to put up a significant amount of cash to get the airplanes that it needs.

For this deal, the Saturn Funding Trust, a fully owned subsidiary of asset-backed lending company WHCO, would acquire the Nvidia GPUs for SpaceX, with the latter paying the former quarterly for the privilege of using the AI chips. The deal is also described as a “five-year triple-net, hell-or-high-water finance lease arrangement,” meaning SpaceX must pay the lease for five years, whether the chips break, become obsolete, or the project becomes unprofitable. It’s also responsible for all the expenses of operating the chips.

Sources indicate that these terms are very lender-friendly, as SpaceX basically assumes all the risks while also keeping them off its books. Rating agency Moody’s also mentioned in its report that the chips will be deployed in SpaceX’s U.S. data centers. Nevertheless, the company’s proposal to blast data centers into space is making some lenders nervous, regardless of its Earth-bound intends and promises.

Today I’m sharing nine of my favorite recent episodes. First, my podcast tool kit I listen with the Snipd app, which lets me mark favorite moments. I triple-tap my AirPods or Sony XM6 headphones to highlight an excerpt. (Why I use Snipd.) Snipd then emails me a summary of my highlights. Readwise hosts my collected podcast notes along with everything else I’ve highlighted while reading online or on my Kindle. Later, I query my clips with Claude or ChatGPT, using the Snipd and Readwise connectors, known as MCPs. (Here’s how that works.) This approach helps me find passages I liked and pull quotes like the ones below. 1. Time-Sensitive Host: Spencer BaileyStandout episode: Oliver Burkeman on the Power of Embracing Imperfectionism I love this podcast’s focus on time. Bailey picks thoughtful guests and asks probing, surprising questions. His thorough research leads to questions other interviewers wouldn’t think to pose. Oliver Burkeman is one of my favorite contemporary authors. I’ve adopted ideas from each of his books, and I make a point of listening to his podcast interviews. So I appreciated that this conversation with Bailey felt different, like the two were venturing into fresh territory. In addition to covering Burkeman’s early career writing for The Guardian, they discussed why we shouldn’t obsess over others’ requests for our time, and how to make peace with imperfection. Bailey is founder of the Slowdown, a collective of writers, editors, photographers, and others focused on quality over quantity. Another great episode: Maria Popova on the role of chance in shaping our lives. The intro to the podcast sums up why Popova’s such a good guest: “The Bulgarian-born, Brooklyn-based . . . founder of the ‘free, ad-free, AI-free, fully human’ website and newsletter The Marginalian braids together literature, science, philosophy, poetry, and art.” 2. How I Work Host: Dr. Amantha ImberStandout episode: Feel Stuck in Small Talk? Daniel Coyle Shares the Questions That Create Real Connection I discovered Daniel Coyle through this episode of Dr. Amantha Imber’s great podcast. He overflows with useful ideas. One of his books, The Talent Code, explores how top performers excel. In a video I like, he summarizes some of its most interesting takeaways. In his conversation with Imber, Coyle offers practical ways to move beyond small talk: Ask better questions, try small community rituals, and notice what gives people energy. 3. Curious Minds at Work Host: Gayle AllenStandout episode: David Epstein on the Power of Limits David Epstein references Dr. Seuss and Apple legend Tony Fadell. His anecdotes spotlight historical figures and contemporary ones. In this interview he draws on themes from his latest book, Inside the Box: How Constraints Make Us Better, to explain how limits help with creativity. Allen is a superb interviewer who asks concise questions and avoids putting herself at the center of the conversation. Subscribe to her podcast for interviews with top contemporary nonfiction writers. Notable quote: “Useful constraints . . . force you to clarify priorities.” —David Epstein 4. The Happiness Lab Host: Dr. Laurie SantosStandout episode: How to Stop Work From Taking Over Your Life I struggle to stop working sometimes, so this episode gave me a lot to ponder. I liked psychologist Guy Winch’s suggestion to treat dreaded tasks like pebbles in our shoes and remove them right away. Thinking of them as nuisances may be helpful in combating procrastination. The episode also suggests planning restorative micro-breaks and building an end-of-work ritual. Notable quote: “We’re taking the 15-minute task, say, 15 minutes of unpleasantness, and we’re smearing it over an entire week.” —Guy Winch 5. The Knowledge Project Host: Shane ParrishStandout episode: Morgan Housel: Wealth Is What You Have Minus What You Want Like Ezra Klein’s, Parrish’s podcast is excellent partly because of the host’s expertise and partly because he picks great guests. Morgan Housel, the interviewee on this episode, is an entertaining storyteller whose first and third books are about the psychology of money. I liked his second most: Same as Ever: A Guide to What Never Changes. Read four of the key points from this episode, or see the full show. 6. Acquired Hosts: Ben Gilbert and David RosenthalStandout episode: Trader Joe’s Each episode of Acquired explores a single manufacturer. Episodes are three to four hours long. The hosts say they spend 100-plus hours doing deep research on each of the eight episodes they publish per year. The depth and quality of their research, reporting, and storytelling have drawn in more than a million listeners. Sponsors pay $500,000 and up, according to a profile of Acquired in The New York Times. There’s even a Harvard Business School case study about their rise. Their marathon episodes challenge the idea that consumers want only short media. This Trader Joe’s episode lasts three hours and 26 minutes. That’s longer than many shoppers spend in the store all year. Listening to Acquired feels like reading an interesting book. The hosts weave lively details about each company they cover into a conversational narrative. Their sharp analysis helps explain how successful ventures stand out. Need to solve a problem? Neuroscience says try the Jack Reacher Method

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1789 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • There’s a point in Lee Child’s book Make Me (the 20th in his Jack Reacher series, for those keeping score) where Reacher is trying to solve a problem and decides to back-burner it: Instead of actively working the problem, he sets it aside, trusting his subconscious to eventually make the right connections.
  • There’s a point in Lee Child’s book Make Me (the 20th in his Jack Reacher series, for those keeping score) where Reacher is trying to solve a problem and decides to back-burner it: Instead of actively working the problem, he sets it aside, trusting his subconscious to eventually make the right connections.
  • Neuroscience demonstrates you tend to be at your most creative when you’re not trying to be creative.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There’s a point in Lee Child’s book Make Me (the 20th in his Jack Reacher series, for those keeping score) where Reacher is trying to solve a problem and decides to back-burner it: Instead of actively working the problem, he sets it aside, trusting his subconscious to eventually make the right connections. Which it does. Sound kinda hokey? Actually, no. Neuroscience indicates you tend to be at your most creative when you’re not trying to be creative. Actually, you’re at your most creative when you’re not trying to do anything at all. Researchers at Washington University in St. Louis used PET scans to determine which parts of the brain lit up during different types of activity. To establish baselines, some participants were put in the scanner and told to do nothing, what the researchers called “resting state.” Surprisingly, resting state resulted in mental energy spikes across various brain regions. In fact, mental energy turned out to be higher in resting state than active state, where participants were given mental tasks. A few years later, neuroscientist Nancy Andreasen made resting-state activity (she called it “free floating periods of thought”) her focus. No tasks. No inputs. No intentional creativity. No nothing; just vegging. As Andreasen writes in The Creating Brain: The Neuroscience of Genius: Most investigators made the convenient assumption that the brain would be blank or neutral during “rest.” From introspection I knew that my own brain is often at its most active when I stretch out on a bed or sofa and close my eyes.We found activations in multiple regions of the association cortex. We were not [seeing] a passive silent brain during the resting state, but rather a brain that was actively connecting thoughts and experiences. Andreasen termed that activity REST: random episodic silent thinking. During REST, Andreasen notes, your brain “uses its most human and complex parts, areas known to gather information and link it all together, in potentially novel ways.” That’s why you sometimes get ideas while taking a walk. Or taking a shower. Or doing dishes. Or driving. When you let your mind wander, when you don’t actively focus on anything specific, your brain makes all sorts of seemingly unconnected associations. You think about the future. You think about the past. You speculate. You synthesize. You test and discard. As Andreasen writes, “When the brain/mind thinks in a free and unencumbered fashion, it uses its most human and complex parts.” In simple terms, if you want to be creative, stop trying to be creative. Stop actively trying to work the problem. Do something relatively mindless, and let your mind do some work in the background. As Steven Johnson wrote in The New York Times: The seemingly trivial activity of mind-wandering is now believed to play a central role in the brain’s “deep learning,” the mind’s sifting through past experiences, imagining future prospects, and assessing them with emotional judgments: that flash of shame or pride or anxiety that each scenario elicits. Granted, REST, or mind-wandering, or whatever you want to call it, is easier stated than done. For one thing, stimulation and “focus” are always within easy reach. Plus, it can feel unproductive, and even oddly uncomfortable, not to fill time with some sort of activity. How many people sit in a waiting room and just wait? How many people sit on a plane and just stare at the seatback in front of them? How many people take a walk without listening to something? How many people don’t listen to something while they’re driving? How many people work out without earbuds? (While it’s just one data point, the other day I went to the gym and counted 18 of 20 people wearing headphones. One of the two not wearing headphones was me.) Sitting and thinking in a “free and unencumbered fashion”? Sounds boring. And it is boring, at least at first. It’s also tough to stick with, especially if you decide to sit in a chair and just stare out the window. So try this instead. Take a walk. (Then you’ll be double-dipping: A study published in the Journal of Experimental Psychology found that your creative output increases by as much as 60% when you’re walking.) Just walk. Don’t think about thinking. Don’t think about what you should be doing, should be listening to, should be focused on. Let your mind wander. In all likelihood, your thoughts will soon drift to a problem you have. Or a challenge you’re working through. Your thoughts will shift forward and backward in time. You’ll sift through hypothetical possibilities and outcomes. You’ll actively, without trying, connect ideas, thoughts, and experiences. When you’re REST-ing, you won’t have to come up with ideas. Ideas will come to you, because that’s how your brain is wired. —By Jeff Haden The opinions expressed here by Inc.com columnists are their own, not those of Inc.com. In simple terms, if you want to be creative, stop trying to be creative. Stop actively trying to work the problem. Do something relatively mindless, and let your mind do some work in the background.

As Steven Johnson wrote in The Upcoming York Times:.

The seemingly trivial activity of mind-wandering is now believed to play a central role in the brain’s “deep learning,” the mind’s sifting through past experiences, imagining future prospects, and assessing them with emotional judgments: that flash of shame or pride or anxiety that each scenario elicits.

Granted, REST, or mind-wandering, or whatever you want to call it, is easier said than done.

For one thing, stimulation and “focus” are always within easy reach. Plus, it can feel unproductive, and even oddly uncomfortable, not to fill time with some sort of activity.

How many people sit in a waiting room and just wait? How many people sit on a plane and just stare at the seatback in front of them? How many people take a walk without listening to something? How many people don’t listen to something while they’re driving? How many people work out without earbuds? (While it’s just one data point, the other day I went to the gym and counted 18 of 20 people wearing headphones. One of the two not wearing headphones was me.).

Sitting and thinking in a “free and unencumbered fashion”? Sounds boring.

In a recent development, and it is boring, at least at first. It’s also tough to stick with, especially if you decide to sit in a chair and just stare out the window.

It has been revealed that so try this instead. Take a walk. (Then you’ll be double-dipping: A study published in the Journal of Experimental Psychology found that your creative output increases by as much as 60% when you’re walking.).

Sources indicate that just walk. Don’t think about thinking. Don’t think about what you should be doing, should be listening to, should be focused on. Let your mind wander.

According to recent reports, in all likelihood, your thoughts will soon drift to a problem you have. Or a challenge you’re working through. Your thoughts will shift forward and backward in time. You’ll sift through hypothetical possibilities and outcomes.

You’ll actively, without trying, connect ideas, thoughts, and experiences.

Industry observers note that when you’re REST-ing, you won’t have to come up with ideas. Ideas will come to you, because that’s how your brain is wired.

—By Jeff Haden.

#149451. NASA’s first 3D printer in space made a wrench. It could help us live on the moon

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fastcompany ↗ Open Full Page

NASA’s first 3D printer in space made a wrench. It could help us live on the moon

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1970 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that one of the newest items to go on display in the National Air and Space Museum in downtown Washington is also one of its most unassuming: a metal box with a glass door on one side, tucked inside a display case dominated by a humanoid robot with arms extended toward the viewer.
  • One of the newest items to go on display in the National Air and Space Museum in downtown Washington is also one of its most unassuming: a metal box with a glass door on one side, tucked inside a display case dominated by a humanoid robot with arms extended toward the viewer.
  • A small white wrench standing next to that box could be even easier to overlook.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that one of the newest items to go on display in the National Air and Space Museum in downtown Washington is also one of its most unassuming: a metal box with a glass door on one side, tucked inside a display case dominated by a humanoid robot with arms extended toward the viewer. A small white wrench standing next to that box could be even easier to overlook. But the wrench was made in that box—a 3D printer developed by Made in Space and flown to the International Space Station as the world’s first experiment in 3D printing while in orbit. NASA spec safety This was not a venture NASA rushed into casually. “They’re definitely cautious,” Michael Snyder, Made in Space’s former CEO, says of the space agency. On Earth, 3D printers can emit tiny particles that get stuck in people’s lungs; on the ISS, there’s no opening a window to clear the air. The answer from Made in Space—a space manufacturing startup that was bought in 2020 by the space hardware manufacturer Redwire—was to place the printing hardware inside that glass-doored enclosure. “That kept everything out of their system,” he says, calling the design mindset “NASA-like caution.” The absence of gravity—technically, “microgravity”—also required modifying standard 3D-printing hardware to yield consistent results; testing was conducted aboard aircraft on parabolic flights to simulate that condition. “Surface tension dominates in microgravity,” Snyder explains. Engineers had to tweak extruder designs to push out feedstock with enough force and deposit each additional layer consistently. Made in Space’s engineers then had to optimize the design for easy operation by astronauts juggling dozens of other tasks. “We wanted it to be a lot more versatile in terms of usability, so you could just swap out canisters of material without even touching any settings,” Snyder says. “All the things are modular in there.” For example, Made in Space designed an extruder head that an astronaut could easily pop out—“like a seat belt, almost, in terms of ease,” Snyder says. And these engineers had to get the printer to sip power. “Basically, we’re taking a device that uses about 1.2 kilowatts of power and shrinking it down,” Snyder recalls—down to a peak power consumption of 196 watts and normal usage of 150 watts. The hardware had to fit inside a single cargo transfer bag (of course NASA has an abbreviation for that: “CTB”) tucked into a SpaceX Cargo Dragon capsule. Says Snyder: “The total volume we had was probably a little larger than a carry-on suitcase.” Ratcheting along Testing proceeded according to a strict script for the first 20 parts, all printed from files already loaded onto the printer. The 21st part would test how it handled uploaded files. “Originally that uplink part was going to be this really easy wire tie,” Snyder recalls. But then Butch Wilmore, one of the astronauts, mentioned that he wished he had his wrench while doing light maintenance on the printer, prompting a change of plans. “At that moment, we were like, we should totally change that uplink part,” Snyder says. They expected NASA to wave off the idea but instead got a green light: “Let’s try it.” But “let’s try it” means something different in the NASA context. To start, the ratchet wrench had to emerge from the printer fully assembled, to avoid the risk of any part breaking away and becoming a source of “FOD” (foreign object damage). Handing over a copy of this wrench, Snyder says, “After about a day and a half we had this.” It feels absurdly light. And then NASA had one last request: a label on the wrench showing its torque rating, in case another astronaut grabbed it and needed to know how much turning force it could apply. With that rating determined, Made in Space was ready to “launch” the wrench to the ISS as an uploaded file. “Day five, we uplinked it, and it was in Butch’s hand later that day”—with a “3 in.-lbs.” label printed in raised letters on the handle. To metal, the moon, and beyond The immediate appeal of being able to fabricate tools and components on demand aboard a spacecraft is reducing the need for Apollo 13-level brainstorming if something goes wrong. But that capability shouldn’t stop at plastic. Made in Space had been planning to follow up on a second printer it had sent to the ISS with a 2020 demonstration of metal “additive manufacturing” in orbit. “We just needed to box it up and put in a payload form,” Snyder recalls. But those plans fell afoul of changing priorities—Snyder isn’t saying whose—leaving it to the European Space Agency to begin the first demonstration of 3D-printed metal aboard the ISS in 2024. NASA’s long-term plans include not just continued human occupancy of space stations in low Earth orbit but also constructing a moon base. Astronauts living and working at a lunar outpost and looking to print their own parts will face a different combination of opportunities and challenges. Or as Snyder puts it: “The moon’s an interesting beast.” Its biggest potential advantage is offering raw materials right outside a moon base’s airlock. “There’s plenty of metal on the moon,” says Snyder. You just have to extract it chemically, through heating or another process: “One of the byproducts in most of the regolith [moon rocks and dust] oxides is usually a metal of some sort.” But lunar gravity being only one-sixth of Earth’s means latest math for calculating hazards like how a flame could propagate. “One-sixth gravity, it turns out, is worse than zero-g in some instances,” Snyder says. Engineers and astronauts will have to figure these things out to make human settlement viable on the moon, some 238,000 miles from Earth Says Snyder: “I don’t think you can sustainably stay on the moon—programmatically or cost wise—without being able to fix stuff.”.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Weekly. Free. One click to leave.

Recent findings suggest that 7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

Picking an ecommerce platform is really a decision about which layers you want to own: the storefront, the catalog and order logic, the payment flow, and the hosting underneath. Every platform below draws that line in a different place. If you have already settled the front-end question with a comparison like SitePoint's Astro vs Next.js guide, the next question is what sits behind it. Prices are from each vendor's pricing page as of November 2026.

Recent findings suggest that shopify is the fully managed option. Basic costs $29 a month with card rates from 2.9% plus 30 cents, and a 2% fee applies to orders processed through a third-party gateway on that blueprint. Developers get two routes: Liquid themes, or Hydrogen, Shopify's headless toolkit, where your framework owns routing and rendering and Hydrogen supplies the Storefront API client and cart. Templates exist for React Router on Oxygen and for Next.js on Vercel. Plus starts at $2,300 a month.

According to recent reports, whop is a business platform for taking payments and sending payouts, and it sits under a storefront you have already built rather than replacing it. The Checkout element runs in the browser with no server code and no API key on the page. You pass your own order ID as metadata, Whop copies it onto the payment, and your server fulfills from a signed webhook that follows the Standard Webhooks spec. Domestic cards cost 2.7% plus 30 cents with no monthly fee, buyers see payment methods chosen by their location across 195 countries, and the same balance pays out in over 200 countries, including to affiliates or sellers you onboard. Whop's own guide highlights how to integrate a checkout API into a Next.js storefront end to end. The trade-off is that there is no catalog or shipping engine; you collect address fields at checkout and trigger fulfillment from the webhook.

WooCommerce is a free plugin on WordPress you host yourself, so you own updates, security, and performance. Its payment gateway, WooPayments, charges US merchants 2.9% plus 30 cents per card transaction, 1.5% more for international cards, 2% for currency conversion, and $25 per dispute. Everything is PHP hooks and filters, which makes it the natural pick for agencies already living in WordPress and the wrong pick for anyone who does not want to run a server.

In a recent development, bigCommerce hosts the back end and lets you bring any front end. Core is $29 a month billed annually, capped at $30,000 in trailing annual sales, and plans auto-upgrade as volume grows. There are no platform fees when you use an embedded payment provider, and a 2% fee on Core if you use another one. Catalyst, its reference storefront, is built on Next.js, React Server Components, and the Storefront GraphQL API, and deploys to Vercel.

Recent findings suggest that medusa is an open-source commerce framework in Node.js and TypeScript, with an MIT-licensed core and a commercial enterprise edition. SitePoint covered it when it was still a young Shopify alternative; it now has over 37,000 GitHub stars. Self-hosting is free. Medusa Cloud starts at $29 a month for development, $99 for launch, and $299 for scale, with no percentage of sales, and the firm indicates you can export your data and self-host at any point.

Saleor is a GraphQL-native, API-only commerce platform written in Python and released under the BSD-3 license. Self-hosting is free. Saleor Cloud starts at $1,599 a month for up to $200,000 in monthly sales, with 0.8% on orders above that, and $3,999 a month at the next tier. It is built for teams with a dedicated engineering function and a large catalog, which is exactly who should pay that price.

Own only the storefront, and Shopify or BigCommerce will carry the rest. Own everything, and Medusa or Saleor give you a back end you can read. Already on WordPress, and WooCommerce is the obvious fit. Already have a storefront in Next.js or Astro and only need the money to move, and Whop is the shortest path. Whichever you pick, the checkout is where disputes start, so log what SitePoint's friendly fraud guide for developers recommends from day one.

#149449. 📚 3LM: A Benchmark for Arabic LLMs in STEM and Code

📅 01 Aug 2025 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (859 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

📚 3LM: A Benchmark for Arabic LLMs in STEM and Code

📅 01 Aug 2025 | ⏱️ 4 min read (859 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • 📄 Paper on arXiv | 📦 Datasets on HuggingFace | 🔧 Code on GitHub.
  • In a recent development, arabic Large Language Models (LLMs) have seen notable progress in recent years, yet existing benchmarks fall short when it comes to evaluating performance in high-value technical domains.
  • Recent findings suggest that to address this gap, we introduce 3LM (علم), a multi-component benchmark tailored to evaluate Arabic LLMs on STEM (Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics) subjects and code generation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

📄 Paper on arXiv | 📦 Datasets on HuggingFace | 🔧 Code on GitHub.

In a recent development, arabic Large Language Models (LLMs) have seen notable progress in recent years, yet existing benchmarks fall short when it comes to evaluating performance in high-value technical domains. Most evaluations to date have focused on general-purpose tasks like summarization, sentiment analysis, or generic question answering. However, scientific reasoning and programming are essential for a broad range of real-world applications, from education to technical problem-solving.

Recent findings suggest that to address this gap, we introduce 3LM (علم), a multi-component benchmark tailored to evaluate Arabic LLMs on STEM (Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics) subjects and code generation. 3LM is the first benchmark of its kind, designed specifically to test Arabic models in structured reasoning and formal logic which are domains traditionally underrepresented in Arabic NLP.

3LM is made up of three datasets, each targeting a specific evaluation axis: real-world multiple-choice STEM questions (MCQs), synthetic high-difficulty STEM questions, and translated code generation tasks.

The Native STEM benchmark consists of 865 MCQs extracted from authentic Arabic educational content, including textbooks, worksheets, and exam banks for grades 8 through 12. Questions span five core subjects: Physics, Chemistry, Biology, Mathematics, and Geography.

It has been revealed that each question is annotated with metadata including domain and difficulty (on a 1–10 scale). The data was sourced using a pipeline that combined OCR (including LaTeX math parsing via Pix2Tex), LLM-assisted question-answer extraction, and manual review. This dataset provides a realistic testbed for evaluating factual and conceptual understanding in Arabic models using real educational materials.

To introduce greater challenge and diversity, we created a synthetic subset of 1,744 MCQs using the YourBench pipeline. This component draws from Arabic textbook text, which is chunked, summarized, and used as input to an LLM-driven question generation system. The result is a curated set of questions focused on mid-to-high difficulty reasoning, including conceptual, analytical, and application-based problems.

Recent findings suggest that synthetic STEM provides an notable counterbalance to native MCQs by probing deeper reasoning skills and minimizing answer bias. All generated questions underwent filtering based on clarity, structure, and content validity, followed by quality assurance via manual review.

In a recent development, the third component of 3LM targets code generation which is a growing area of LLM evaluation. We translated and adapted the widely-used HumanEval+ and MBPP+ benchmarks into Arabic, creating the first code datasets that test Arabic LLMs on natural language prompts for programming.

We used GPT-4o for prompt translation and validated the results with a backtranslation pipeline, rejecting low-quality samples based on ROUGE-L F1 thresholds (< 0.8). Additional human filtering ensured prompt clarity and correctness. The code and test suites remain unchanged to preserve scoring fidelity. Evaluations use the EvalPlus framework for pass@1 and pass@1+ metrics.

Each dataset in 3LM went through a multi-stage development process to ensure data quality, fairness, and representativeness.

According to recent reports, for Native STEM, we collected Arabic PDF sources and applied a dual OCR approach to recover both plain text and math formulas. Questions were extracted using LLM-based chunking and pattern recognition, followed by classification into MCQ format with randomized answer order. Final samples were reviewed by native Arabic speakers with STEM expertise to confirm answer validity and readability.

It has been revealed that for Synthetic STEM, the YourBench pipeline was adapted for Arabic input. Source documents after ingestion were first summarized, chunked and then fed to a code-controlled generator for MCQ creation. We filtered out image-dependent or ambiguous content, and only retained questions within target difficulty ranges. The result is a set of clean, high-quality synthetic Arabic MCQs for STEM.

It has been revealed that for the Code Benchmarks, our goal was to isolate language understanding while preserving code logic. Prompt translation was handled by GPT-4o with verification via reverse translation. Code and tests were untouched to allow evaluation parity with English versions. The result is a benchmark where Arabic prompts can be evaluated directly with the EvalPlus toolchain.

Sources indicate that we evaluated over 40 LLMs, including Arabic-first, multilingual, and general-purpose base and instruction-tuned models. Evaluation was performed using both multiple-choice accuracy and generative completion metrics.

In the MCQ setting, Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct achieved top performance across both native (71.8%) and synthetic (67.0%) STEM subsets. For completion tasks, Gemma-3-27B demonstrated the strongest results with 43.2% accuracy on STEM answers.

In code generation, GPT-4o demonstrated best-in-class performance on both HumanEval-ar (83.5% pass@1+) and MBPP-ar (63.6% pass@1+). These results highlight strong correlation (~0.97) between Arabic and English pass@1 scores, suggesting language-specific prompt quality has a major influence on model outcomes.

Industry observers note that we also examined robustness under distractor perturbation, revealing that instruction-tuned models are significantly more stable than their base counterparts. Prompt engineering and zero-shot design were also shown to meaningfully affect Arabic STEM performance.

We built the benchmark to be easily reproducible using standard tools:.

All scripts, configs, and evaluation pipelines are available in our GitHub repository, and can be adapted to evaluate any model compatible with HuggingFace Transformers or OpenAI APIs.

All three datasets are open-source and hosted on HuggingFace Datasets:.

If you use 3LM in your research, please cite us:.
