AI-powered bionic eye breakthrough could help the blind see again

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1465 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that artificial intelligence could help overcome one of the biggest challenges in restoring vision to people who are blind: getting a brain implant to produce reliable visual experiences.
  • It has been revealed that the team used a deep learning system to develop electrical stimulation patterns for electrodes temporarily implanted in the visual cortex, the region at the back of the brain responsible for processing visual information.
  • Published online in the journal Neuron, the proof-of-concept study represents progress toward more advanced visual prostheses, sometimes described as bionic eyes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that artificial intelligence could help overcome one of the biggest challenges in restoring vision to people who are blind: getting a brain implant to produce reliable visual experiences. Researchers from three institutions, including UC Santa Barbara, have demonstrated that AI can improve how precisely an experimental visual prosthesis stimulates the brain and predicts what a person perceives.

It has been revealed that the team used a deep learning system to develop electrical stimulation patterns for electrodes temporarily implanted in the visual cortex, the region at the back of the brain responsible for processing visual information. By analyzing the brain's responses, the technology gave researchers greater control over neural activity and helped them better anticipate the visual sensations produced by the implant.

Published online in the journal Neuron, the proof-of-concept study represents progress toward more advanced visual prostheses, sometimes described as bionic eyes. These devices could eventually become more effective by learning how each person's brain responds to stimulation rather than relying on predetermined settings.

According to recent reports, "Building a model in the abstract is one thing," said Michael Beyeler, an associate professor of computer science and psychological and brain sciences at UC Santa Barbara. "Seeing it shape an experiment with a person is something else entirely. That ability to go from theory to something that may one day help people is what drives much of the work in our lab.".

How Bionic Vision Could Bypass Damaged Eyes.

Sources indicate that for decades, scientists have worked to develop technologies capable of restoring some vision to people who are blind, although the results have generally been limited. Some experimental devices stimulate the retina, the layer of tissue at the back of the eye that detects light. Others attempt to activate parts of the visual system farther along the pathway that carries visual information to the brain.

Sources indicate that visual cortical prostheses work differently. Instead of depending on the eyes or optic nerves, they deliver electrical signals directly to the visual cortex. This approach could offer a potential solution for people whose visual pathways have been damaged but whose visual cortex can still respond to stimulation. Possible candidates include individuals who lost their sight because of strokes, neurodegenerative diseases, or traumatic brain injuries.

The ability to regain even limited vision could be especially meaningful for people who remember what it was like to see.

Beyeler highlighted those "who have been able to see for part of their life, but then, because of an inherited eye disease or an accident, have lost their vision," adding, "For those people, the desire may be very strong to get some vision back.".

The new findings build on earlier computational research supported by Beyeler's 2022 National Institutes of Health (NIH) Director's New Innovator Award. The five-year, $2 million grant has supported his efforts to make artificial vision systems more accurate, predictable, and effective.

Scientists Test AI With a Brain Implant in a Blind Man.

An crucial opportunity to test the technology came in 2024, when researchers from Beyeler's Bionic Vision Lab traveled to Spain. Their goal was to determine whether their computer models could improve the performance of a brain implant already being used in an experimental study.

Sources indicate that at Hospital IMED Elche, the team worked with a 27-year-old man who had become blind following a traumatic brain injury. He had received an implant containing 96 electrodes arranged in an array within his visual cortex. The device was intended to remain in place for six months before being removed.

Sources indicate that when researchers activated the electrodes using electrical current, the participant experienced visual sensations known as phosphenes. These can appear as spots, flashes, or shapes of light, sometimes resembling stars or fireworks.

According to recent reports, producing these sensations is possible, but making them consistent and predictable is much more difficult. The same electrical stimulation does not always trigger an identical response, and activating particular electrodes does not guarantee that the person will perceive a specific visual pattern.

It has been revealed that to address this problem, the researchers trained a deep neural network, a type of AI designed to recognize complex patterns, to predict how the visual cortex would respond to different electrical stimulation settings. The model also considered the brain's resting activity immediately before stimulation, giving it information about the participant's current neural state.

Using these predictions, the researchers identified combinations of electrical signals that were most likely to produce particular patterns of brain activity.

AI Makes Bionic Vision More Precise.

Recent findings suggest that when the scientists tested the stimulation patterns selected by AI, the results were encouraging. The latest approach generated the intended patterns of neural activity more accurately than the comparison methods while requiring less electrical current.

Sources indicate that another important discovery emerged when the team examined the relationship between brain activity and the participant's visual experiences. The patterns recorded directly from his brain were better predictors of what he perceived than the stimulation settings themselves.

It has been revealed that this distinction matters because activating the brain is not the same as knowing what a person will see. Even when researchers can produce a desired neural response, they still need to understand how the brain transforms that activity into a conscious visual experience.

Sources indicate that "Engineers naturally want to treat phosphenes like pixels: stimulate more electrodes, and you should get a more complete image," Beyeler mentioned. "But the brain does not work that way. Electrodes interact, neural responses fluctuate, and what we put into the brain is not necessarily what the person perceives. The challenge is to learn more about that transformation.".

The findings suggest that future visual prostheses may need to do more than simply deliver electrical signals. They may also need to monitor how the brain reacts and use that feedback to continually improve stimulation.

Teaching Brain Implants to Adapt to Each Person.

A key advantage of the implant used in the experiment was its ability to perform two tasks. It could stimulate the visual cortex with electrical current while simultaneously recording the resulting neural activity.

This allowed researchers to train their AI model using the brain's actual responses rather than relying exclusively on information about which electrodes were activated and how much current they delivered.

The participant also provided feedback about what he experienced. He reported whether he saw a phosphene and, during certain experiments, described its appearance, including its shape, size, brightness, and color.

Comparing these reports with the recorded brain activity revealed that neural responses contained more useful information about the perceived visual sensations than the electrical stimulation parameters alone.

It has been revealed that the AI system also used measurements of resting brain activity to account for changes in the participant's neural state before each stimulation. This could be particularly valuable because the brain's response to electrical signals can vary over time, including from one day to the next.

By adapting stimulation to these changing conditions, future prostheses might provide more consistent visual experiences without requiring customers to adjust to a rigid set of signals.

"A useful visual prosthesis cannot rely on a fixed recipe," Beyeler mentioned. "It has to learn how an individual brain responds and adapt the stimulation accordingly. Ultimately, the device should adapt to the person, not the other way around.".

A Collaborative Step Toward Restoring Sight.

The research brought together scientists from UC Santa Barbara, ETH Zurich, and Miguel Hernández University (MHU). Beyeler described the effort as "a true collaboration.".

The project was led by co-first authors Pehuén Moure of ETH Zurich, Jacob Granley of UC Santa Barbara, and Fabrizio Grani of MHU. The supervising researchers were Beyeler, Shih-Chii Liu of ETH Zurich, and Eduardo Fernández of MHU. Their work forms part of a larger feasibility trial taking place in Spain.

Although the technology remains experimental and the participant's visual experiences were limited to flashes and shapes of light, the results demonstrate how AI could improve communication between artificial vision devices and the brain.

According to recent reports, rather than treating every brain as if it responds the same way, future bionic vision systems could learn from each individual and adjust their signals accordingly. That personalized approach may prove essential to developing implants that can eventually restore useful vision to people who have lost their sight.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Moore Threads’ MTT S80 product manager says that the next Lushan gaming GPU will have more VRAM than any consumer graphics card currently available, VideoCardz reports.
  • Moore Threads apparently hasn’t given up on graphics, even four years after the MTT S80’s release.
  • Although nothing the product manager stated is an official statement, his words suggest that the newly introduced Lushan GPU could feature the largest memory capacity yet offered on a consumer graphics card, which certainly draws a lot of attention from gamers and local AI enthusiasts alike.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Moore Threads’ MTT S80 product manager says that the next Lushan gaming GPU will have more VRAM than any consumer graphics card currently available, VideoCardz reports. With Nvidia’s RTX 5090 already at 32GB, Lushan would need more than that. This matches the previous promise of four times the organization’s MTT S80’s 16GB, putting the flagship Lushan at 64GB.

Moore Threads apparently hasn’t given up on graphics, even four years after the MTT S80’s release. The company teased the card earlier this week with a poster for MDC 2026, its developer conference, showing a graphics card under a black cloth on a mountainside, and put Lushan’s name in the title of the post. It has previously indicated that Lushan products would arrive before the end of the year.

Although nothing the product manager stated is an official statement, his words suggest that the newly introduced Lushan GPU could feature the largest memory capacity yet offered on a consumer graphics card, which certainly draws a lot of attention from gamers and local AI enthusiasts alike. As it stands, the 32GB RTX 5090 was available at $6,599 in our recent Newegg check, more than three times its MSRP, which illustrates the astronomical demand.

Not disclosed; “4x” the S80 claimed, up to 64GB by our math.

$1,999 MSRP; from $6,599 at Newegg (Nov. 15).

2,999 yuan with a motherboard (about $410) at launch; 1,499 yuan (about $225) at JD.com, Nov. 21.

Intel Arc Pro B60 Dual (Maxsun).

Sources indicate that the Lushan would be a graphics rendering chip based on the Huagang architecture, with a sibling Huashan for AI. Performance claims are lofty at 15x for AAA gaming, 50x ray tracing, 64x AI compute, and 16x geometry processing over the MTT S80, based on information from MDC 2025, last year’s edition of the conference. To get there, Lushan adds a fresh hardware ray-tracing engine, the UniTE rendering architecture, AI generative rendering, which MyDrivers describes as the manufacturer’s answer to Nvidia’s DLSS and AMD’s FSR for upscaling and multi-frame generation, and DirectX 12 Ultimate support.This is a mighty high goal, as the previous outing, with the S80, fell short of expectations. Released in November 2022 at 2,999 yuan (about $410), the S80 was at first sold only in a bundle with an Asus motherboard. It now costs about half that in China, despite rising GPU costs. The 16GB GDDR6, PCIe 5.0 GPU, which pulls 255W, only matched a low-end card when tested on immature drivers in early 2023; it struggled against a GT 1030.

Moore Threads noted last December that it had shipped monthly driver updates since and claimed the S80 then benchmarked 3.4x higher than at launch. The upcoming 15x target is more reasonable when put against the backdrop of just how far the S80 trailed when it landed.

If we look beyond the consumer space, there are plenty of cards that have more than 32GB, and 64GB for that matter. The Nvidia RTX Pro 6000 Blackwell workstation card, for instance, has 96GB of GDDR7. It’s also possible to get RTX 4090s rebuilt with 48GB, at least in some Chinese shops, and a listing in September offered an RTX 5090 modded to 96GB. Maxsun also has the Arc Pro B60 Dual, built on Intel GPUs, with 2x 24GB on just one board. However, memory supply remains tight, with crushing memory shortages, and is projected to remain so, while GDDR7 remains quite costly.

Domestic rival Lisuan’s G100, meanwhile, is only at 12GB and 24GB for consumer and enterprise. A 64GB Lushan would leave those in the dust, which may hint that Moore Threads is targeting Western cards rather than just domestic rivals. It also raises the question of just how much memory you need for certain workloads.

Tech Report: How a Los Angeles freeway became home to the world’s largest wildlife bridge

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2291 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • How do you design a bridge that a mountain lion mistakes for a hillside?
  • How do you design a bridge that a mountain lion mistakes for a hillside?
  • Industry observers note that the crossing—the largest of its kind in the world—won’t officially open until December 2, and even after that point, some construction and habitat restoration will still be underway around the main structure.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

How do you design a bridge that a mountain lion mistakes for a hillside? That’s the design challenge behind the massive new Annenberg Wildlife Crossing, which stretches across 10 lanes of the 101 freeway northwest of Los Angeles. The crossing—the largest of its kind in the world—won’t officially open until December 2, and even after that point, some construction and habitat restoration will still be underway around the main structure. But animals have already started using it, from a coyote to lizards and Western bluebirds. Around 450 species live in the area. It’s not yet known how many animals will cross the bridge each year, though for apex predators like mountain lions, even a few crossings a year could be crucial to the populations’ survival. Getting it right took more than a decade of planning and design work. It was the opposite of a typical infrastructure project, with greenery as an afterthought after the concrete is in place. “All of the infrastructure is there in service of this habitat connection,” indicates Robert Rock, CEO of Rock Design Associates, the lead landscape architect behind the Annenberg Wildlife Crossing. [Photo: Caltrans] Reconnecting a fragmented ecosystem The project is helping restitch an ecosystem that was split apart by the freeway. To the south is sprawling open space in the Santa Monica Mountains; to the north, there’s more protected land that indirectly connects to the Angeles National Forest. The new crossing includes the main bridge across the freeway, a second smaller bridge across a nearby road, and around 13 acres of habitat restoration. Before the bridge existed, data showed that most wildlife that approached the freeway would turn around. The road, with around 300,000 cars passing every day, makes it nearly impossible for animals to cross. That’s especially a problem for mountain lions, since young male mountain lions need to be able to find new territory. A 2016 study found that the fragmented habitat and inbreeding meant that mountain lions faced steep population decline and a 99.7% chance of local extinction within 50 years. Conservation groups suggested the idea of a crossing as early as the 1980s, and Caltrans, the state transportation department, started studying the idea in 2003. But there wasn’t dedicated funding to build it. Despite more studies, the project stalled. Photographer Steve Winter holds his iconic photo during a memorial for P-22 at the Greek Theatre in Los Angeles, California, on February 4, 2023. [Photo: Robyn Beck/AFP/Getty Images] A turning point came in 2013, when a mountain lion living in Griffith Park, surrounded by L.A.’s urban sprawl, was photographed under the Hollywood sign and went viral. Known as P-22, the lion had managed to cross the 101 freeway, his tracking data showed. The National Wildlife Federation and the Santa Monica Mountains Fund made P-22 the face of a new campaign for a crossing, and funding started to pour in. By 2019, final design work was underway. [Photo: Caltrans] A ‘giant green roof’ The main bridge, at 250 feet wide, is designed to be substantial enough to comfortably accommodate all the different species that might need to cross it, from bobcats and mountain lions to rabbits and squirrels. The size is based on research from other wildlife crossings—like one in Banff National Park in Canada, where elk and grizzly bears use a bridge over a highway. (The U.S. Federal Highway Administration’s design guidelines suggest that crossings should be at least 130 feet wide.) The designers worked carefully with scientists to understand what different species in the area needed to feel comfortable crossing. “This was a huge kind of professional translation between us on the design side and the biologists on the science side,” says Rock. [Image: NWF and Rock Design Associates] Small prey animals need connected plantings to scurry through without open space; deer need open pathways so they have a clear view of what’s ahead. In between plantings on the bridge, there’s a path made of aggregate that can keep plants from spreading and preserve some open space. The bridge recreates native coastal sage habitat in what Rock compares to a “giant green roof.” Because the crossing sits in the middle of the area that burned in a huge wildfire in 2018, the team is also carefully restoring habitat leading up the bridge. The team collected more than a million seeds from other wild areas nearby, then grew plants in its own nursery. [Photo: Caltrans] Due to the fire’s extreme heat, fungi and microorganisms in the top 14 inches of soil in the area were destroyed, leading the team to take samples of healthy soil from elsewhere in order to make something that Rock compares to sourdough starter. As the area is replanted, the soil biology will be restored. (The plants were chosen with fire resiliency and heat tolerance in mind; the area will also be irrigated with recycled water, which can be used to help protect it when the next wildfire happens.) It was an unusual project for the Caltrans planting crew, says Rock, because they normally work on fairly simple plantings next to highways. The design team planned it out in a grid, with a mix of native plants in each square arranged in the same way they would be in nature. [Photos: National Park Service] Making the crossing quiet and dark One of the biggest challenges for the new crossing was the location. Because it’s a major highway, both sound and light pollution were much bigger problems than in a place like Banff, which is an isolated national park. [Image: NWF and Rock Design Associates] “We have ambient sound levels that are the equivalent of a rock concert on the north side and maybe a folk concert on the south side,” says Rock. “We needed to find a way to create additional quiet space and additional dark spaces along the freeway.” The team worked with an acoustical engineer who designed software to help them explore approaches to sound reduction. Terraced embankments under the bridge help deflect traffic noise and absorb low-frequency sounds. Along the sides of the bridge, planters with sloping walls also help shield animals from noise and light. The design reduces noise by 20 decibels, compared to 5-10 decibels for an ordinary highway sound barrier. Because sound is measured logarithmically, that’s a huge difference. [Photo: Caltrans] Since light bounces off concrete, creating the urban phenomenon called “sky glow” at night, the designers avoided using standard gray or white concrete for the bridge. Instead, it’s a dusty brown that helps keep the area darker. The team also asked Caltrans to swap out standard bright white LED streetlights for warmer yellow lights near the bridge. Earlier in the construction process, after the basic structure of the bridge was put in place, biologists visiting the site at night watched as a barn owl flew back and forth in the newly dark strip across the freeway. “It’s one of those things that at that early stage just gave us all chills,” Rock says.

How do you design a bridge that a mountain lion mistakes for a hillside? That’s the design challenge behind the massive new Annenberg Wildlife Crossing, which stretches across 10 lanes of the 101 freeway northwest of Los Angeles.

Industry observers note that the crossing—the largest of its kind in the world—won’t officially open until December 2, and even after that point, some construction and habitat restoration will still be underway around the main structure. But animals have already started using it, from a coyote to lizards and Western bluebirds. Around 450 species live in the area. It’s not yet known how many animals will cross the bridge each year, though for apex predators like mountain lions, even a few crossings a year could be crucial to the populations’ survival.

Getting it right took more than a decade of planning and design work. It was the opposite of a typical infrastructure project, with greenery as an afterthought after the concrete is in place. “All of the infrastructure is there in service of this habitat connection,” indicates Robert Rock, CEO of Rock Design Associates, the lead landscape architect behind the Annenberg Wildlife Crossing.

The project is helping restitch an ecosystem that was split apart by the freeway. To the south is sprawling open space in the Santa Monica Mountains; to the north, there’s more protected land that indirectly connects to the Angeles National Forest. The new crossing includes the main bridge across the freeway, a second smaller bridge across a nearby road, and around 13 acres of habitat restoration.

Before the bridge existed, data highlighted that most wildlife that approached the freeway would turn around. The road, with around 300,000 cars passing every day, makes it nearly impossible for animals to cross. That’s especially a problem for mountain lions, since young male mountain lions need to be able to find new territory. A 2016 study found that the fragmented habitat and inbreeding meant that mountain lions faced steep population decline and a 99.7% chance of local extinction within 50 years.

It has been revealed that conservation groups suggested the idea of a crossing as early as the 1980s, and Caltrans, the state transportation department, started studying the idea in 2003. But there wasn’t dedicated funding to build it. Despite more studies, the project stalled.

In a recent development, A turning point came in 2013, when a mountain lion living in Griffith Park, surrounded by L.A.’s urban sprawl, was photographed under the Hollywood sign and went viral. Known as P-22, the lion had managed to cross the 101 freeway, his tracking data showed. The National Wildlife Federation and the Santa Monica Mountains Fund made P-22 the face of a new campaign for a crossing, and funding started to pour in. By 2019, final design work was underway.

The main bridge, at 250 feet wide, is designed to be big enough to comfortably accommodate all the different species that might need to cross it, from bobcats and mountain lions to rabbits and squirrels. The size is based on research from other wildlife crossings—like one in Banff National Park in Canada, where elk and grizzly bears use a bridge over a highway. (The U.S. Federal Highway Administration’s design guidelines suggest that crossings should be at least 130 feet wide.).

The designers worked carefully with scientists to understand what different species in the area needed to feel comfortable crossing. “This was a huge kind of professional translation between us on the design side and the biologists on the science side,” says Rock.

Small prey animals need connected plantings to scurry through without open space; deer need open pathways so they have a clear view of what’s ahead. In between plantings on the bridge, there’s a path made of aggregate that can keep plants from spreading and preserve some open space.

The bridge recreates native coastal sage habitat in what Rock compares to a “giant green roof.” Because the crossing sits in the middle of the area that burned in a huge wildfire in 2018, the team is also carefully restoring habitat leading up the bridge. The team collected more than a million seeds from other wild areas nearby, then grew plants in its own nursery.

It has been revealed that due to the fire’s extreme heat, fungi and microorganisms in the top 14 inches of soil in the area were destroyed, leading the team to take samples of healthy soil from elsewhere in order to make something that Rock compares to sourdough starter. As the area is replanted, the soil biology will be restored. (The plants were chosen with fire resiliency and heat tolerance in mind; the area will also be irrigated with recycled water, which can be used to help protect it when the next wildfire happens.).

It has been revealed that it was an unusual project for the Caltrans planting crew, says Rock, because they normally work on fairly simple plantings next to highways. The design team planned it out in a grid, with a mix of native plants in each square arranged in the same way they would be in nature.

One of the biggest challenges for the new crossing was the location. Because it’s a major highway, both sound and light pollution were much bigger problems than in a place like Banff, which is an isolated national park.

“We have ambient sound levels that are the equivalent of a rock concert on the north side and maybe a folk concert on the south side,” says Rock. “We needed to find a way to create additional quiet space and additional dark spaces along the freeway.”.

The team worked with an acoustical engineer who designed software to help them explore approaches to sound reduction. Terraced embankments under the bridge help deflect traffic noise and absorb low-frequency sounds. Along the sides of the bridge, planters with sloping walls also help shield animals from noise and light. The design reduces noise by 20 decibels, compared to 5-10 decibels for an ordinary highway sound barrier. Because sound is measured logarithmically, that’s a huge difference.

Since light bounces off concrete, creating the urban phenomenon called “sky glow” at night, the designers avoided using standard gray or white concrete for the bridge. Instead, it’s a dusty brown that helps keep the area darker. The team also asked Caltrans to swap out standard bright white LED streetlights for warmer yellow lights near the bridge.

Recent findings suggest that earlier in the construction process, after the basic structure of the bridge was put in place, biologists visiting the site at night watched as a barn owl flew back and forth in the newly dark strip across the freeway. “It’s one of those things that at that early stage just gave us all chills,” Rock says.

  • It has been revealed that NVIDIA’s AI-Q Blueprint—the leading portable, open deep research agent—recently climbed to the top of the Hugging Face “LLM with Search” leaderboard on DeepResearch Bench.
  • It fuses two high-performance open LLMs—Llama 3.3-70B Instruct and Llama-3.3-Nemotron-Super-49B-v1.5—to orchestrate long-context retrieval, agentic reasoning, and robust synthesis.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Contributors: David Austin, Raja Biswas, Gilberto Titericz Junior, NVIDIA.

It has been revealed that NVIDIA’s AI-Q Blueprint—the leading portable, open deep research agent—recently climbed to the top of the Hugging Face “LLM with Search” leaderboard on DeepResearch Bench. This is a significant step forward for the open-source AI stack, proving that developer-accessible models can power advanced agentic workflows that rival or surpass closed alternatives.

The greatest strength of the James Bond brand isn’t its consistency. It’s its ability to reinvent itself while remaining unmistakably Bond. With Robert Pattinson confirmed as the next 007, the debate has inevitably turned to whether he’s the right man for the role. But I think there’s a much more interesting question. What should Bond represent today? The best brands know when to change James Bond has never stood still. Ian Fleming’s original character was ruthless, brutal, and considerably less glamorous than the sophisticated figure we’ve come to recognize. Every generation has reinvented him. Sean Connery brought a working-class edge to an establishment character. Roger Moore introduced humor and extravagance. Pierce Brosnan was polished, almost to the point of parody. And Daniel Craig stripped much of that away, giving us a more grounded, vulnerable, and human Bond. Pierce Brosnan [Photo: Keith Hamshere/Getty Images] The shift from Brosnan to Craig was striking. It challenged what audiences expected from Bond, and arguably made him more relevant. That’s something iconic brands often struggle with. They become so protective of their heritage that they forget what made them successful in the first place. Heritage should give brands the confidence to move forward, not make them a museum to the past. Daniel Craig [Photo: Greg Williams/Eon Productions/Getty Images] Recognizable doesn’t mean unchanged James Bond has an extraordinary collection of brand assets. The cars and gadgets, the suits and theme music, the villains and their lairs, the martini order and the gun-barrel opening. But none of these is Bond on its own. The franchise has continually reinterpreted these elements to reflect changing ideas of technology, sophistication, and masculinity, without losing its identity. Bond’s gadgets are a perfect example. By the Brosnan era, a fascination with gadgets had become full-blown fantasy, epitomized by the invisible Aston Martin in Die Another Day. Craig’s Bond, meanwhile, marked a return to practicality, with his biometrically locked pistol in Skyfall. Throughout, the underlying idea remained the same: Bond could rely on Q to give him a technological edge. It was the interpretation of that that changed, not its importance. Sean Connery and Daniela Bianchi in From Russia, With Love. [Photo: Bettmann/Getty Images] Take the villains, for example. They’ve often reflected the feeling of their time. The Cold War shaped films like From Russia With Love, while Skyfall explored the threat of cyberterrorism and the vulnerability of intelligence systems. The threats changed, but the role they played in making Bond relevant remained the same. The franchise’s relationship with sexual politics has evolved, too. Compare Honey Ryder’s famous emergence from the sea in Dr. No with Daniel Craig’s in Casino Royale. Romantic conquests with absurd names, over time, became professional equals like Nomi. When Judi Dench’s M dismissed Bond as a “sexist, misogynist dinosaur” in GoldenEye, it was an early recognition that even 007’s most established behaviors could be challenged as cultural expectations evolved. Roger Moore [Photo: Michael Ochs Archives/Getty Images] Heritage is a starting point, not a constraint Louis Vuitton is a good example of a brand that understands this distinction. Founded as a trunk maker in 1854, it could have become increasingly irrelevant as the nature of travel changed. Instead, it expanded into handbags, fashion, and accessories while retaining its association with craftsmanship, luxury, and the romance of travel. Timothy Dalton [Photo: Keith Hamshere/Getty Images] Its original purpose has evolved, but the brand continues to draw on its travel heritage through its products, visual identity, campaigns, and experiences. Its distinctive monogram, originally developed for its luggage, has become one of the most recognizable symbols in luxury. Louis Vuitton didn’t need to keep making trunks its primary business to remain Louis Vuitton. It understood what made the brand valuable and found latest ways to express it. That’s the difference between being recognizable and being relevant. The best brands understand that you can protect what makes you distinctive without preserving everything exactly as it was. [Photo: Francesco Francavilla/Variety/Penske Media/Getty Images] What kind of Britain does Bond represent now? James Bond has always been more than a film franchise. He’s one of Britain’s most recognizable cultural exports, shaping how the country is perceived around the world. One of the best examples was the London 2012 Olympics opening ceremony, when Daniel Craig’s Bond appeared alongside Queen Elizabeth II. It was a brilliant moment that captured a particular version of Britain: confident, creative, playful, and comfortable enough with its heritage to laugh at itself. But Britain today is a very different place: Brexit, the transition from queen to king, economic pressures, and growing questions about class and national identity have all changed the cultural landscape. Which makes Pattinson’s casting particularly interesting. Connery and Craig brought a grittier, more grounded quality to Bond. Pattinson comes from a more privileged background, raising the question of whether the franchise is returning to a more traditional, establishment view of Britishness. Of course, an actor’s upbringing doesn’t determine the character he plays. But casting is a creative choice that can signal what a brand wants to represent. At a time when many people feel increasingly disconnected from the establishment, what kind of Bond will feel relevant? And what version of Britain do we want to project to the world? Robert Pattinson [Photo: Lia Toby/Getty Images for BFI] Reinvention is about relevance The challenge for Pattinson, director Denis Villeneuve, and Amazon MGM Studios isn’t simply to make another successful James Bond film. It’s to decide what should remain, what needs to change, and what Bond means to a new generation. Because the greatest risk for an iconic brand isn’t changing too much. It’s becoming so protective of its past that it stops being relevant to the future.

AI agents design an entirely fresh CPU architecture from scratch, startup claims

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1115 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that architect Labs, a Palo Alto startup, mentioned in a research blog post that its AI systems discovered, designed, and verified Frostbite, a general-purpose CPU with a new instruction set “built from the ground up.” Across 25 workloads, a four-tile Frostbite cluster delivered 4.59 times the performance per watt of a similarly sized “silicon-proven” dual-glitch, in-order CPU core.
  • It has been revealed that conventional CPUs have hardware that “rediscovers, at runtime, which instructions actually depend on each other.” Multicore designs also need deep cache hierarchies and coherence protocols, which keep every core’s view of shared memory consistent, but scale poorly and cost area and power.
  • Recent findings suggest that frostbite’s programs are compiled to interaction nets, a model of computation from 1990 in which a program is a graph of nodes and computation happens by rewriting pairs of connected nodes, and the chip is designed around this distinct paradigm.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that architect Labs, a Palo Alto startup, mentioned in a research blog post that its AI systems discovered, designed, and verified Frostbite, a general-purpose CPU with a new instruction set “built from the ground up.” Across 25 workloads, a four-tile Frostbite cluster delivered 4.59 times the performance per watt of a similarly sized “silicon-proven” dual-glitch, in-order CPU core. Those numbers come from a simulated 7nm design that has not yet been made in silicon, and the organization claims it can’t name the comparison core for legal reasons.

It has been revealed that conventional CPUs have hardware that “rediscovers, at runtime, which instructions actually depend on each other.” Multicore designs also need deep cache hierarchies and coherence protocols, which keep every core’s view of shared memory consistent, but scale poorly and cost area and power. Architect Labs’ alternative is what it calls “multithreading for free,” where the program itself exposes the parallel work, without threads, locks, or out-of-order hardware required for that discovery.

Recent findings suggest that frostbite’s programs are compiled to interaction nets, a model of computation from 1990 in which a program is a graph of nodes and computation happens by rewriting pairs of connected nodes, and the chip is designed around this distinct paradigm. Pairs of nodes being rewritten never overlap, so they can run in any order, or all at once, and arrive at the same result. Every value is also used exactly once, so data can stay in small local memories instead of large shared caches.

An example of the difference given by the team is a 5x5 chess-like board with five queens, placed so none can attack another. A typical program searches for solutions one board at a time. As an interaction net, the same search breaks into 3,183 small operations, and the longest chain that has to run in order is only 262 steps, so on average about 12 operations are ready to run at once at each step. Nothing about the program was rewritten to get there, as the parallel work was already intrinsic.

It has been revealed that each of the chip’s tiles, small identical processing units linked by an on-chip network, has its own small local memory. Four tiles, plus four L3 nodes, form the cluster that’s benchmarked against the conventional core for the performance claims, but the full layout has 16 tiles. The design reached 800 MHz in early synthesis but ended up at 500 MHz in the final layout. The cluster also averaged 8.77 times the comparison core’s performance per area, and the table below demonstrates how its performance per watt varies by workload.

It has been revealed that frostbite performance per watt vs. comparison core.

15 held out until the final evaluation.

Worst: recursive Fibonacci (held out).

It may come as some surprise that the AI which built Frostbite started with what the tech giant calls “zero architectural priors,” though the team first picked the workloads it had to do well on, and this sort of blank slatism may have its advantages in avoiding bias. Instead, the agents read papers and benchmarks, built Python models, and then selected one concept for focus. The original 141-page PDF output, which contained a programming model, runtime, and high-level blocks, was deleted after the first register-transfer level (RTL) design was generated, because “many of the numbers and estimates were well off what was physically possible.”.

That PDF was only ever a starting point. Once the agents picked an architecture, they moved away from English — as it can’t get every detail right or catch every mistake, according to the team — and wrote the spec in the company’s own language, called ASL. ASL translates to Lean, a proof checker, so it can be machine-checked, which the company notes stops a large class of bugs and cuts down on agents gaming their objectives. From this, the agents devised Arcmodel, a software model of the whole chip written in ASL, before any circuit design existed.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Recent findings suggest that simulating the RTL is slow, so the agents tested ideas on the model instead, which ran about 200 times faster. At first, the model’s power estimates were off by up to almost 250%, but an automated loop adjusted it until it matched the circuit design within just 5%.

From there, swarms of agents proposed changes in parallel, and each one was checked against the spec, tried in the fast model, built into the circuit design, and measured for power before being kept or dropped. This led to 58 ideas tried, with 37 kept. Separately, a behavior emerged that “was never specified by any human,” in what is known as work stealing: a tile with nothing to do can pull spare work from a neighbor or, in lieu of anything to do, go idle to save power.

Share of energy (one four-tile cluster, mean of 20 workloads, excluding clock distribution).

Fetching, decoding, and issuing instructions.

Clock distribution (share of total energy, left out of the rows above).

This isn’t Architect Labs’ first design, as it indicated off Redwood, an AI inference accelerator for robots and drones, in August. In that case, the manufacturer indicates its AI generated the RTL, verification, firmware, drivers, and kernels in under two weeks from a spec written by two human architects. Redwood still runs only on an FPGA and hasn’t been made in silicon, though the company says it is working toward having it built at TSMC.

Tendrils Compute, a possible rival based in Cambridge, U.K., raised funding earlier this month for a processor it says will have “thousands of cores operating in parallel.” It is also developing Vine, the same language Frostbite’s programs are written in.

According to recent reports, architect Labs indicates more benchmarks are coming, but they’re only part of the strategy. It also wants an FPGA-hosted “software playground for anybody to run a program on Frostbite” along with a “preliminary operating system.” Eventually, it intends to release Frostbite’s RTL and instruction set.

In the meantime, the company plans to cover more workloads and compare “a broader set of CPUs,” including larger Frostbite mesh configurations against multicore versions of the comparison core with large caches. It also plans to test against “larger, wider, out-of-order CPUs,” with these comparisons due in the coming months on popular CPU benchmark suites such as SPEC and PARSEC.

Breaking: 6 ways to use AI to shop smarter—without giving it access to your wallet

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Thanksgiving is fast approaching, which means Black Friday is too.
  • Recent findings suggest that thanksgiving is fast approaching, which means Black Friday is too.
  • Recent findings suggest that personally, I’m not a Black Friday shopper.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Thanksgiving is fast approaching, which means Black Friday is too. In the era of AI-assisted shopping, tech companies offer tools that allow you to shop directly on their platforms, or through integrations with online retailers and payment providers. Personally, I’m not a Black Friday shopper. I also don’t feel comfortable giving an AI model my credit card information (or letting it invest for me or make other financial transactions on my behalf). But I do feel comfortable sharing low-stakes information about my needs and interests and stretching a model’s search capability to its limit. Treating my chatbot like a research assistant has saved me time and money, and helped me avoid the annoyance of navigating online stores. Below are a few tips for using artificial intelligence to shop more efficiently, without handing over your credit card information to a bot. Use AI to find exactly what you need, faster Shopping online can be a nightmare, especially if you need something really specific. Say you need to find a bookshelf that fits in a space with very specific dimensions. Why waste time sifting through myriad websites—and endless advertisements—when AI can search for a product that meets your exact needs? The same goes for everything from household repair items to bridesmaid dresses of a certain hue: AI saves you time by searching for exactly what you need, whether that’s a certain size, color, or operating system. And it’s less mentally taxing than going through an endless number of websites. Tell AI where you have a subscription—and where you don’t Many of us have subscriptions to services we prefer, and platforms we prefer to avoid. Telling AI where you already have memberships, and where you might even be collecting points, can help you shop more efficiently. If you’re part of a loyalty program and have a credit card from Lowe’s, there’s little reason for AI to recommend products from Kmart or Walmart. Tell your AI where you like to shop and have it tailor its results accordingly. This might involve telling AI that you want links only from Costco, not Amazon, or that you prefer to read suggestions from Fast Firm, where you have a login (ahem). This advice also applies to frequent flyer miles and credit card rewards. Have AI search for coupons and other cost-saving measures Use AI to find coupon codes and other money-saving opportunities. This isn’t any special application of AI, but simply involves exploiting the powerful search capabilities of large language models to benefit your wallet. About to buy an expensive product? Ask a model where else you can buy it, and whether it’s available for less. You might even ask it to investigate whether a purchase qualifies for reimbursement through a Flexible Spending Account, and what documentation you’d need. Develop a shopping plan with AI Sometimes you really want to see something in person before you buy it. AI can help you come up with an itinerary of stores to check out in person, and direct you to the best neighborhoods for window shopping. It can also help you prioritize your time and travel, drawing up efficient routes and suggesting the best time of day to head out. Ask AI for suggestions Perhaps there’s a product that will make your life better and you just don’t know it yet. AI might have some good ideas, though. It can also help you find reviews that speak to specific concerns you might have about a product, searching the web more thoroughly. This might mean investigating whether anyone has complained about safety problems with, say, a robotic cat litter box, or searching for resort reviews written by parents who can speak to how well a place works for families. Help understand warranties and refunds Sometimes a purchase that seemed perfect turns out to be anything but. AI can help you navigate complicated warranty and refund policies—and potentially get your money back. Have it review the terms of your purchase, identify the strongest grounds for a refund, and even draft a persuasive request on your behalf.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A new computational technique could accelerate the search for diamond materials capable of powering future quantum computers and highly sensitive sensors. Developed by a researcher at the U.S. Department of Energy's (DOE) Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory (PPPL), the method makes it much easier to identify promising materials for quantum technology, potentially opening the door to advances across many areas of science.

Industry observers note that the approach has already revealed upcoming candidates for quantum computing and sensing applications. The findings were recently published in ACS Central Science and have attracted attention from other researchers in the field.

Industry observers note that one of the biggest challenges in developing quantum technology is finding materials that can maintain delicate quantum states under practical conditions. Many candidates require extremely low temperatures to function reliably. Diamond materials stand out because certain quantum properties can remain useful even at room temperature.

This capability could help advance technologies that are notable to national research priorities and the development of next-generation computing. Quantum sensors promise levels of sensitivity and precision beyond those of conventional instruments, while quantum computers could eventually solve certain extraordinarily complex problems much faster than today's most powerful supercomputers.

Why Imperfect Diamonds Could Be the Key to Quantum Computing.

Although diamonds are made of carbon atoms, a flawless diamond crystal is not enough to create a useful quantum computing system. The key lies in tiny irregularities within the crystal structure.

These imperfections, known as defects, can occur when a carbon atom is absent from its normal position, when another element replaces a carbon atom, or when both changes occur together. The atoms surrounding these defects can form qubits, the basic units used to store and process quantum information in quantum computers and sensors.

Finding the most useful defects, however, has been difficult. Accurately modeling their quantum behavior traditionally requires enormous computational resources, making it challenging to evaluate large numbers of possible candidates.

A Simpler Way to Discover Better Diamond Qubits.

Mark Martirez, a staff research scientist at PPPL, developed a way to dramatically reduce the complexity of these calculations. Instead of simulating a much larger diamond structure, he isolates a small region containing just 16 to 30 atoms around a defect.

It has been revealed that by "carving out" this tiny atomic cluster and treating it like a separate molecule, Martirez can use powerful computational methods that chemists have spent decades refining. These established techniques make it possible to analyze the quantum properties of diamond defects much more efficiently without sacrificing the high level of accuracy needed for the calculations.

"Because we're treating the qubits as molecules, the cost of calculating these defects is equivalent to the cost of just modeling a simple molecule," Martirez mentioned. "This method really opened the floodgates" in terms of how qubits can be assessed.

It has been revealed that the new technique allows researchers to calculate how different qubits respond to laser light and microwave pulses far more quickly than before. Using this approach, the team identified promising defects involving boron and oxygen that could serve as new types of qubits.

Newly introduced Diamond Defects Reveal a Spectrum of Quantum Colors.

Industry observers note that light plays an key role in how scientists interact with diamond qubits. Researchers use lasers and microwave pulses to manipulate their quantum states and retrieve stored information.

Much of the previous work in this area has centered on a defect known as the nitrogen-vacancy center. This structure forms when a nitrogen atom takes the place of a carbon atom in a diamond crystal, while an adjacent position that would normally contain another carbon atom remains empty.

Under laser illumination, this type of defect can emit red light when it occupies a particular quantum state.

In a recent development, the newly investigated defects offer different optical properties. Oxygen defects can produce blue light, while those involving boron emit ultraviolet light.

It has been revealed that these differences could make it possible to combine several types of qubits within a single quantum device. Because each type responds differently to light, researchers might be able to interact with one group of qubits without disturbing another.

"One could imagine, then, combining different qubits of different responses, so you can basically probe one qubit but not the other," Martirez said.

Beyond identifying upcoming candidates, the findings suggest a broader change in how researchers approach quantum technology. Diamond qubits have traditionally been studied primarily through physics, but understanding their underlying chemistry could provide additional ways to design them.

Martirez believes that researchers could eventually engineer qubits for particular functions using principles similar to those applied when chemists create specialized molecules, including compounds designed for latest medications.

How Quantum Chemistry Could Transform Future Research.

The potential benefits extend well beyond the development of quantum computers themselves. Martirez sees an intriguing possibility in which advances made possible by quantum chemistry eventually lead to quantum technologies that help improve the field of chemistry.

In other words, quantum chemistry could develop the very tools needed to "enrich itself" in the coming decades.

Industry observers note that A practical quantum system containing multiple qubits could make molecular calculations substantially more accurate. That would allow scientists to study increasingly complex chemical structures, including large biological molecules and proteins, with a level of detail that is difficult to achieve using conventional methods.

Recent findings suggest that "We could describe larger molecules, biomolecules, proteins and everything like that in a more accurate way, and that could improve all the chemical-adjacent industries, such as pharmaceutical science and materials science. Even our fundamental understanding of molecular systems could be enriched.".

Such improvements could have far-reaching implications for pharmaceutical development, materials research, and the fundamental study of how molecules behave.

Recent findings suggest that martirez also hopes the research will encourage more chemists to explore solid-state physics. Although building advanced quantum computers is often viewed as a challenge primarily for physicists, he argues that chemistry offers valuable expertise that could help accelerate progress.

Sources indicate that "At this moment in time, there's a great emphasis on building the first state-of-the-art qubit computer," he said. "But it's not just physicists who should be participating in this research. Chemists have decades of developed intuition about chemical systems that could be easily translated into understanding defects in solids as well.".

By bringing these disciplines together, scientists may be able to develop more effective ways to discover, understand, and eventually engineer the quantum materials needed for future technologies.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that A federal judge on Wednesday extended a temporary block on President Donald Trump’s proposed monumental arch just outside Arlington National Cemetery, and the stopped clock gives the public more time to reflect on Trump’s intends for the land.
  • A federal judge on Wednesday extended a temporary block on President Donald Trump’s proposed monumental arch just outside Arlington National Cemetery, and the stopped clock gives the public more time to reflect on Trump’s intends for the land.
  • There’s a consensus that a 250-foot-tall structure is a misfit for the site.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that A federal judge on Wednesday extended a temporary block on President Donald Trump’s proposed monumental arch just outside Arlington National Cemetery, and the stopped clock gives the public more time to reflect on Trump’s intends for the land. There’s a consensus that a 250-foot-tall structure is a misfit for the site. But maybe an alternative project might be better suited to it? A pair of landscape architecture students think it could become a circular reflecting pool. The current site. [Photo: Duane Lempke/Wikimedia Commons.] Memorial Circle, where Trump wants to build the arch, is for now an empty roundabout. It sits between Arlington Cemetery to its southwest and the Lincoln Memorial just across the Potomac to its northeast. Despite its location between popular tourist destinations, it’s not designed for pedestrians to access. [Image: © Jeremy Dvorak and Jake Geitner/courtesy The Cultural Landscape Foundation] The two alternative designs for what to do with the circle, released this week by the Cultural Landscape Foundation, a nonprofit education and advocacy group, imagine the space in upcoming ways. One concept turns the circle into a single, circular reflecting pool, making the Lincoln Memorial a hinge between two reflecting pools; the other imagines it as a larger park configured as pedestrian-friendly, civic space. [Image: © Jeremy Dvorak and Jake Geitner/courtesy The Cultural Landscape Foundation] “We are having right now in Washington a crisis of imagination and also an inability to understand that Washington is a mosaic of spaces that people move through in the public realm,” Charles A. Birnbaum, founding president and CEO of the foundation, tells Fast Tech giant. “The projects that we’ve been seeing from the administration, whether it’s the ballroom or the arch or the Garden of Heroes [a statue park proposed for parkland south of the Lincoln Memorial], they’re all being forced upon the civil and cultural landscape of Washington.” The foundation’s two alternative design provocations were made in collaboration with Jeremy Dvorak and Jake Geitner, landscape architecture students in a class Birnbaum teaches at the Harvard University Graduate School of Design. Both proposals use water to convey monumentality instead of sheer height, as in Trump’s proposal. Trump’s proposed 250-foot arch would tower above D.C.’s maximum 130-foot height limit. The project is being sued by veterans, who say it will block the sight line from the cemetery to the Lincoln Memorial, meant to symbolize national reunification after the Civil War, as well as by Arlington County, the Commonwealth of Virginia, and the District of Columbia, who’ve argued it’s unauthorized. It’s also unpopular. Two-thirds of Americans, including half of Republicans, oppose Trump’s dedicating time and energy to construction projects like the arch, according to a Reuters-Ipsos poll conducted last month. Neither of the students’ proposals rise to a level that would block anyone’s view. [Image: © Jeremy Dvorak and Jake Geitner/courtesy The Cultural Landscape Foundation] The first alternative proposal would turn Memorial Circle into a circular reflecting pool meant to be viewed by passing cars. The pool purposely sits at a low elevation so you can see it at car level, since there’s no safe passage to cross the street as a pedestrian in its current configuration. It’s a minimalist, modest monument for motorists that keeps Memorial Circle’s function intact while simultaneously elevating it as a space for reflection. Words conveying unity and belonging would be inscribed in a granite profile enclosing the reflecting pool. [Image: © Jeremy Dvorak and Jake Geitner/courtesy The Cultural Landscape Foundation] The second alternative proposal would reconfigure the roundabout, turning the Memorial Avenue corridor into a pill-shaped park for pedestrians. Anchored by two fountain pools with high water sprays, the park would have trees and benches ringing the outside, giving tourists and visitors shade and seating. The lack of a single focal point for this idea was purposeful, Birnbaum states. It becomes a processional experience between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington Cemetery. Instead of an arch or other central element that reveals itself, it serves as a midpoint that visually and environmentally ties the cemetery to the National Mall. [Image: © Jeremy Dvorak and Jake Geitner/courtesy The Cultural Landscape Foundation] Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act of 1966 requires an assessment of adverse effects of any projects on historic federal properties, and these proposals more closely follow that mandate than a grand arch does, Birnbaum says. “The letter of the law is to avoid, minimize, and mitigate adverse effects,” he says. He also argues they more closely follow Interior Secretary Doug Burgum’s stated rationale for the project, which is “to reinforce the historical and ceremonial role of the Arlington Memorial Bridge and Memorial Avenue corridor as a symbolic gateway between Washington, D.C., and Arlington National Cemetery, while providing a new destination for public interpretation, reflection, and appreciation of the nation’s history.” For the students and foundation, these proposals are just a starting point. “This is about fostering a dialogue, but also addressing what we feel is a lack of imagination,” Birnbaum says.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, GPT OSS is a hugely anticipated open-weights release by OpenAI, designed for powerful reasoning, agentic tasks, and versatile developer use cases. It comprises two models: a significant one with 117B parameters (gpt-oss-120b), and a smaller one with 21B parameters (gpt-oss-20b). Both are mixture-of-experts (MoEs) and use a 4-bit quantization scheme (MXFP4), enabling fast inference (thanks to fewer active parameters, see details below) while keeping resource usage low. The large model fits on a single H100 GPU, while the small one runs within 16GB of memory and is perfect for consumer hardware and on-device applications.

To make it even better and more impactful for the community, the models are licensed under the Apache 2.0 license, along with a minimal usage policy:.

We aim for our tools to be used safely, responsibly, and democratically, while maximizing your control over how you use them. By using gpt-oss, you agree to comply with all applicable law.

In a recent development, according to OpenAI, this release is a meaningful step in their commitment to the open-source ecosystem, in line with their stated mission to make the benefits of AI broadly accessible. Many use cases rely on private and/or local deployments, and we at Hugging Face are super excited to welcome OpenAI to the community. We believe these will be long-lived, inspiring and impactful models.

It has been revealed that openAI GPT OSS models are accessible through Hugging Face’s Inference Providers service, allowing you to send requests to any supported provider using the same JavaScript or Python code. This is the same infrastructure that powers OpenAI’s official demo on gpt-oss.com, and you can use it for your own projects.

GPT OSS models are reasoning models: they therefore require a very large generation size (maximum number of upcoming tokens) for evaluations, as their generation will first contain reasoning, then the actual answer. Using too small a generation size risks interrupting the prediction in the middle of reasoning, which will cause false negatives. The reasoning trace should then be removed from the model answer before computing metrics, to avoid parsing errors, especially with math or instruct evaluations.

Here’s an example on how to evaluate the models with lighteval (you need to install from source).

For the 20B model, this should give you 69.5 (+/-1.9) for IFEval (strict prompt), and 63.3 (+/-8.9) for AIME25 (in pass@1), scores within expected range for a reasoning model of this size.

If you want to do your custom evaluation script, note that to filter out the reasoning tags properly, you will need to use skip_special_tokens=False in the tokenizer, in order to get the full trace in the model output (to filter reasoning using the same string pairs as in the example above) - you can discover why below.

Sources indicate that openAI GPT OSS uses the concept of “channels” in its outputs. Most of the time, you will see an “analysis” channel that contains things that are not intended to be sent to the end-user, like chains of thought, and a “final” channel containing messages that are actually intended to be displayed to the user.

Assuming no tools are being used, the structure of the model output looks like this:.

Most of the time, you should ignore everything except the text after <|channel|>final<|message|>. Only this text should be appended to the chat as the assistant message, or displayed to the user. There are two exceptions to this rule, though: You may need to include analysis messages in the history during training or if the model is calling external tools.

Recent findings suggest that when training: If you’re formatting examples for training, you generally want to include the chain of thought in the final message. The right place to do this is in the thinking key.

You can feel free to include thinking keys in previous turns, or when you’re doing inference rather than training, but they will generally be ignored. The chat template will only ever include the most recent chain of thought, and only in training (when add_generation_prompt=False and the final turn is an assistant turn).

The reason why we do it this way is subtle: The OpenAI gpt-oss models were trained on multi-turn data where all but the final chain of thought was dropped. This means that when you want to fine-tune an OpenAI gpt-oss model, you should do the same.

According to recent reports, openAI GPT OSS is unusual because it distinguishes between a “system” message and a “developer” message at the start of the chat, but most other models only use “system”. In GPT OSS, the system message follows a strict format and contains information like the current date, the model identity and the level of reasoning effort to use, and the “developer” message is more freeform, which makes it (very confusingly) similar to the “system” messages of most other models.

Recent findings suggest that to make GPT OSS easier to use with the standard API, the chat template will treat a message with “system” or “developer” role as the developer message. If you want to modify the actual system message, you can pass the specific arguments model_identity or reasoning_effort to the chat template:.

Industry observers note that GPT OSS supports two kinds of tools: The “builtin” tools browser and python, and custom tools supplied by the user. To enable builtin tools, pass their names in a list to the builtin_tools argument of the chat template, as shown below. To pass custom tools, you can pass them either as JSON schema or as Python functions with type hints and docstrings using the tools argument. See the chat template tools documentation for more details, or you can just modify the example below:.

If the model chooses to call a tool (indicated by a message ending in <|call|>), then you should add the tool call to the chat, call the tool, then add the tool result to the chat and generate again:.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that hello and welcome to Modern CEO! I’m Stephanie Mehta, CEO and chief content officer of Mansueto Ventures. Each week this newsletter explores inclusive approaches to leadership drawn from conversations with executives and entrepreneurs, and from the pages of Inc. and Fast Company. If you received this newsletter from a friend, you can sign up to get it yourself every Monday morning. I was in Silicon Valley for part of last week, where many investors, founders, and executives seem to shrug off the midterm elections, in which voter distrust of big tech and AI safety played a role in the blue wave. Their conclusion? Data centers—those massive, resource-heavy computing facilities—simply have a “PR problem.” They maintain that the tech sector needs to launch a charm offensive to remind communities of all the good that will come from these massive computing facilities, such as jobs and support for small businesses. Heck, the tech giants might even send some employees to volunteer at local schools! A growing concern  This interpretation of the election results is naively narrow and largely misses the point. “Data centers are the foil,” says Jim O’Leary, CEO of the global advisory firm Penta. “They’re the face of the AI backlash, but the matter is bigger.” Indeed, a Pew Research Center report published in August found that 52% of Americans stated they are more concerned than excited about the use of artificial intelligence in daily life, up from 37% in 2021. Sentiment analysis from Penta found that negative press coverage of AI safety rose 233% from May to October of this year versus from November 2025 to April 2026. All that translates into lawmakers focusing their attention on AI and the companies that are building and deploying the technology. Nearly half (46%) of policymakers interviewed by Penta in the weeks prior to the midterm elections said safety and responsibility were their top AI concerns—and government interest in AI is only going to grow in the run-up to 2028. “I think AI will be the defining issue of the general election,” O’Leary says. Beyond data centers   Some of the scenarios O’Leary is contemplating make the data center backlash seem almost quaint. Over the next 24 months, he foresees one or more of the following AI-related crises: a safety incident that could involve loss of life, an AI market correction or outright bubble burst, or a cyberattack larger than those we’ve recently seen. If all three scenarios materialize, “it will create an environment that is extraordinarily complicated,” O’Leary says. “A significant portion of the population will push for an AI slowdown. And business leaders will need to ask, ‘How do we continue to drive AI transformation across our business, which we know we have to do?’”  Even business leaders who have a strong conviction to expand AI usage in their companies will bump up against stakeholders such as employees and community leaders who may want to pump the brakes. Leaders will need to engage in conversations with all of these groups to understand objections and, where possible, work together to overcome them. After two years of courting the White House, big businesses will need to build bridges with an emboldened legislative branch. Says O’Leary: “Corporations are now going to have to start prioritizing congressional engagement in a way they didn’t over the past 24 months.”  Modern CEO of the year  Modern CEO is seeking nominations for the 2026 Modern CEO of the Year. If you or a CEO you know has had an exceptional year driving innovation, transforming a business, or future-proofing a company, please share their story via this form. The deadline for submissions is December 4, and the Modern CEO (or CEOs) of the Year will be unveiled on December 28. Quantum computers are getting too powerful to check. Scientists have a solution

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that as quantum computers grow more powerful, researchers face a troubling question: How can they know whether the results are correct when conventional computers can no longer verify them?
  • The technique uses experimental measurements to reconstruct how a quantum system behaves, then calculates how uncertainties in that reconstruction affect the results.
  • In a recent development, quantum systems are expected to become capable of solving increasingly complex problems that traditional computers struggle with or cannot handle at all.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that as quantum computers grow more powerful, researchers face a troubling question: How can they know whether the results are correct when conventional computers can no longer verify them? Scientists have now developed a promising new method that could help overcome this challenge by measuring the accuracy of quantum simulations and identifying how much uncertainty their predictions contain.

The technique uses experimental measurements to reconstruct how a quantum system behaves, then calculates how uncertainties in that reconstruction affect the results. Researchers successfully demonstrated the approach using a quantum simulator with up to 51 qubits in Innsbruck, Austria.

In a recent development, quantum systems are expected to become capable of solving increasingly complex problems that traditional computers struggle with or cannot handle at all. However, this progress creates a verification problem. When a simulation is small enough, scientists can compare its results with calculations performed on a conventional computer. As quantum systems grow beyond those limits, that direct comparison becomes impractical, making alternative ways to assess their reliability essential.

A Newly introduced Way to Measure Quantum Computing Accuracy.

It has been revealed that the breakthrough comes from an international research team led by Tristan Kraft at the Technical University of Munich and Peter Zoller at the University of Innsbruck and the Institute for Quantum Optics and Quantum Information of the Austrian Academy of Sciences, working alongside Barbara Kraus of the Technical University of Munich. The researchers developed a method for experimentally determining how a quantum simulator operates and translating uncertainties in its behavior into measurable limits on the accuracy of its results.

According to recent reports, quantum simulators are specialized physical systems designed to reproduce the behavior of other quantum systems. They are especially useful for investigating situations involving large numbers of interacting particles, where the calculations required can swiftly overwhelm even powerful conventional computers.

But quantum experiments are never entirely free from errors. "But no real experiment is perfect," notes Tristan Kraft. "Interactions may turn out differently than expected, the system is influenced by its environment, and measurements are also subject to uncertainties.".

It has been revealed that rather than assuming a quantum simulator behaves exactly as intended, the latest approach examines experimental data to determine what is actually happening inside the system. This allows researchers to identify notable interactions and account for disturbances such as fluctuations and noise.

Industry observers note that "From this data, we determine the relevant interactions as well as key influences from fluctuations and noise. We then calculate how the uncertainties in this model affect the simulation results," explains Tristan Kraft. "The quantum simulator thus provides not just a single value, but a result with error margins that quantify its accuracy.".

Successfully Tested on a 51 Qubit Quantum Simulator.

Recent findings suggest that to evaluate the method, the researchers began with a relatively small quantum system containing ten trapped ions. Because conventional computers can still calculate the behavior of a system of this size, the team could test its reconstructed models and calculated error limits against independent measurements.

Sources indicate that after this initial validation, the researchers expanded their experiments to a chain of 51 trapped ions. The larger demonstration, carried out by a team led by Manoj Joshi and Christian Roos using an ion trap quantum simulator, highlighted that the technique could also work with substantially more complex quantum systems.

This represents an crucial step toward establishing how trustworthy quantum simulation results are, particularly as quantum devices advance into territory where direct verification with traditional computing methods becomes increasingly difficult.

Extending the Breakthrough to More Complex Quantum Systems.

It has been revealed that the next challenge is to bring the technique to two-dimensional quantum simulators. These systems can model more complicated interactions among particles, making them valuable for exploring quantum physics. At the same time, their growing complexity makes their results particularly difficult to confirm using conventional calculations.

"This is particularly key because classical calculations for such systems become significantly more difficult as the number of particles increases," explains quantum computing pioneer Peter Zoller. "This also makes independent verification of the results increasingly complex, making the question of experimentally determined error limits all the more important.".

The researchers are now adapting their method for the newest generation of two-dimensional quantum simulators, which offer improved precision and can investigate systems containing larger numbers of particles.

Looking further ahead, the approach could help scientists establish a more meaningful way to measure quantum advantage, the ability of quantum systems to outperform conventional computers. Instead of comparing machines based only on their processing speed or the size of the problems they can handle, researchers could also examine how accurately each system produces its answers.

Industry observers note that "After all, when a classical computer and a quantum simulator tackle the same problem, it's not just a matter of which one delivers a result faster. What's also crucial is which one can solve the problem with a smaller, verifiable margin of error," notes Peter Zoller.

Recent findings suggest that this shift could change how progress in quantum computing is evaluated. Future breakthroughs may be judged not simply by how many particles a simulator can model or how rapidly it performs calculations, but by its ability to solve increasingly difficult problems with demonstrably reliable results.

In a recent development, the findings were published in Physical Review X. The research received support from the Austrian Science Fund (FWF), the German Ministry of Research, Technology and Space, the European Union, BMW, and other funding organizations.

TSMC reportedly pauses shipments to Chinese designers after U.S. export rules flag decade-old 16nm and 14nm nodes
